articles.title: Retro tech meets modern AI: Inside an Amazon developer’s garage turned working computer museum
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Darko Mesaros used to park a car in the garage of his Maple Valley, Wash., home. These days, it’s wall-to-wall computers.
A towering server rack glows with red LEDs. CRT monitors are stacked beside vintage workstations, and a workbench overflows with tools, cables, and half-repaired components.

“I started getting stuff, and then … it just kind of snowballed to a point I actually had to slow down because I legitimately don’t have space for it anymore,” Mesaros told GeekWire during a recent tour of his retro hardware labyrinth.

The lore of tech innovation is full of suburban garages where visionary founders tinkered their way to world-changing companies. Mesaros, a distinguished developer advocate at Amazon Web Services, isn’t launching a startup out of his. Instead, he’s using it as a living museum to rescue, repair, and resurrect the discarded digital ghosts of computing history — and then daring them to run modern artificial intelligence.

The collection has spilled into an upstairs office and now spans more than 100 full computers, from an early-1970s minicomputer to Silicon Graphics workstations from the ’90s and HP workstations from the 2000s. Add roughly 25 vintage video game consoles, rescued software, peripherals, a leather-bound TRS-80 owner’s manual, and nearly a decade of 1980s Byte magazines, and the total tops 1,000 items.
Most of it arrives broken, and that’s the point.
“Buying a mint old system is not fun,” he said. “Buying something that’s broken and then having that excitement of fixing it is just fantastic.”

He finds gear at Goodwill, through local Facebook Marketplace groups, and through Seattle’s large retro computing community. Sometimes it takes a rescue mission: when a man in Washington, D.C., was about to throw away a pallet of 1980s computers, Mesaros had a friend there grab it, then paid to ship the whole load to Seattle.
At one point, he had seven Commodore 64s. He gives extras to other collectors, and he’s never sold a single piece.
Mesaros’ fascination with vintage hardware goes beyond nostalgia; it’s the foundation of a lifelong obsession with how things work under the hood.

Growing up in Serbia, he faced an economic reality where cutting-edge tech was out of reach. From 1991 to 2003, his only computer was a Commodore 64 — a machine released in 1982. While the rest of the computing world sped through the 1990s and early 2000s, Mesaros skipped straight to modern PCs.
“I feel like I missed that whole thing,” he said. “I missed the whole, you know, Sun workstation, Silicon Graphics, HP 9000, all of those things … and I just wanted to explore how that was.”
So he bought a couple of Sun workstations to see what he’d missed. Then he kept going.
“It’s a hobby, but it’s also a problem,” he said with a laugh.
If the garage caught fire, the one machine he’d grab? A bright blue Silicon Graphics Indy, the 1990s workstation from the very era he missed growing up. It was the first SGI he bought.
“It showed me how this amazing workstation worked!” he said. He still fires it up from time to time just to enjoy its IRIX operating system.
Still on his wish list: a DEC VT520 terminal with an amber screen. Working units only seem to turn up on the East Coast, and he won’t risk shipping a fragile CRT across the country.

Before joining Amazon nearly a decade ago, he held system administration and engineering roles at companies including AT&T and Tipico. Now at AWS, his day job involves leveraging his experience to help developers and customers adopt and use AWS services via blogs, webinars, code, and technical advocacy. The garage doubles as his set: he records AWS videos and live streams there.

Mesaros moved to the Seattle area around the start of the pandemic, arriving with a couple of workstations, a monitor, and a handful of laptops before his collection expanded. He soon realized gear was far cheaper here than in Europe.

“Most of these things are older than me. Especially older than my tech career,” the 38-year-old noted. “Actually, all of these things are older than my career. However, again, I find it fascinating how computer history has evolved.”

His arrival timing meant he narrowly missed the chance to visit Seattle’s beloved Living Computers: Museum + Labs before it permanently closed its doors . But in his own home, he’s essentially built a private version of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s former institution.
Beyond the vintage hardware, Mesaros’ appreciation for computing history is permanently etched onto his body.

He sports a collection of retro tech tattoos on his arms, including symmetrical DOS and Linux terminal prompts (C:\WINDOWS> and root@localhost), a classic Windows 95 logo, MS-DOS branding, a shebang and a quit command that mark the start and end of a script, and detailed microprocessors like the Zilog Z80 and MOS 6502 paired with assembly code — a setup he jokingly calls his literal “ARM CPUs.” He’s still waiting, he said, on his check from Microsoft.

“I only tattoo ancient technology on myself,” Mesaros said, noting that people frequently stop him at airports to take pictures. “Old technology will stay with me … I feel like this is an investment in my career.”
He has plans for more ink during his next trip home to Serbia.

For Mesaros, collecting vintage computers is about more than admiring silent plastic shells on a shelf; it’s about making them talk across the digital chasm. In his garage and upstairs office, he routinely bends ancient hardware to modern purposes — proving that an 8-bit machine or a mechanical teletype can still interface with the cutting-edge cloud.

Mesaros has chatted with an AI coding agent from a Commodore 64 and deployed Kubernetes via a 1986 Tandy 102 portable computer. He wired a 1984 DEC DECwriter IV teletype to Amazon’s Kiro coding agent, explaining in a blog post how he talks to Kiro through the clacking machine — and he’s even deployed AWS infrastructure from it.
“Should this be done? Probably not,” he said. “But is it fun? Absolutely.”

In a demo for GeekWire, we watched the teletype clatter out the agent’s answer to his query, “What is GeekWire?” After a few seconds of hammering, it printed: “Seattle-based tech news site covering Pacific Northwest startups, Amazon, Microsoft and the broader tech industry.”
Not bad for a machine older than its operator.
Mesaros also spent a weekend trying to get stuck in 1999, using a Windows 98 machine as his only computer and documenting it on a VHS camcorder.
“The only window into the future was Kiro,” he said.

While these stunts might sound like elaborate practical jokes, Mesaros believes they serve a vital purpose in the age of AI. In a modern development landscape where tools let programmers “build a to-do app and walk away,” he argues that developers are losing the art of paying attention.

He likes to point out that a 2017 Google paper titled “Attention Is All You Need” helped kick off today’s LLM boom. “Now in 2026, to be a really successful developer,” he said, “attention is all you need.”

“I think being curious and paying attention are the two most important skills for a developer these days because it is so easy not to do those things,” Mesaros said. “And if you want to be relevant, if you want to be good at your job, especially with AI, I think those are the two important things that are critical.”

When he isn’t troubleshooting an obscure serial card data-ready pin or attempting to hook up a military field phone from his native Serbia to an LLM, he balances his digital obsession with analog pursuits. He wrenches on an old Jeep TJ — parked in the driveway because there’s no room in the garage.
He’s not the only tinkerer in the house. His wife is a fashion designer who 3D prints clothing and purses on a farm of printers in one of the upstairs rooms.
“She’s more creative than I am,” he said. “I get to tinker with old things that don’t want to work, and she uses technology to actually make new things.”

When it comes to the tech he lets into his own life, Mesaros is choosy. He wears a classic analog Timex and bought Meta’s smart glasses when they came out — then sold them within a month. “I don’t like the camera on my face,” he said. (He does use a camera-free pair that can display real-time translated subtitles when he travels abroad.)

That same instinct is why he doesn’t see screens going away, even as AI agents take on more work. “We still have the need for control,” he said. “Being able to observe and see, visualize what’s happening is still important.”

articles.title: How ICE Continues to Wield Washington's Own Data
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: In the wake of accelerated immigration enforcement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) across the country this summer and into fall, new data shows that Washington state driver data is still being used to enable and assist in these arrests.

The update comes from the University of Washington Center of Human Rights (UWCHR), which published an initial report at the beginning of the year showing how Washington state driver data was being accessed to assist in federal immigration enforcement. Now, nine months later, UWCHR has data showing this practice has continued unabated. Researchers have confirmed 356 arrest incidents between August 1, 2025 and October 13, 2026 that have resulted from federal agents receiving Washington State Department of Licensing (DOL) driver data through the interstate querying system Nlets.

“We know that 356 is likely only a small fraction of the total cases that are happening,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy at a press conference on Tuesday. “Those are just the ones where we were able to confirm it with smoking gun evidence connecting a given plate search to a known immigration arrest.”
ICE continues to access this DOL data in spite of the 2019 Keep Washington Working Act and government officials being aware of this data access pathway since at least 2018, according to the report.

Federal agents’ general operating procedure is to travel to target-rich environments where they think they might find immigrants. They ask the state for data about certain license plates via Nlets, run the registered owner names they are given via Nlets through their own databases, and then decide whether to make an arrest.

Nilu Jenks, a candidate for the District 5 seat of the Seattle City Council, wants to add the Seattle Police Department’s use of Nlets to the Office of the Inspector General’s annual surveillance review while also calling for action from the state legislature and Governor Bob Ferguson.

“In District 5, ‘target rich’ is a polite way of saying racial profiling,” said Jenks. “It means agents deciding who looks deportable by the color of their skin and the work truck they drive: the roofer outside a hardware store on Aurora, the landscaping crew in Maple Leaf, the dad dropping his kids at school in Lake City. When a license plate becomes a name and home address in moments, every trip is a risk. Nobody should have to wonder whether it's safe to drive because of how they look, and no state database should help put a target on their backs.”
Godoy underlined that Washington state hasn’t been doing enough to address the increasing levels of violence and fear experienced by immigrant residents.

“This is a time of extraordinary pain and difficulty for immigrant communities in Washington and around our country, not only because we are experiencing unprecedented levels of immigration enforcement here in the region and around the country, but also because we're experiencing the use of increasingly violent tactics, which appear to involve overt racial profiling, often warrantless arrests, which challenge the Constitution,” Godoy said. “Multiple courts around the nation have found these practices to be unconstitutional, in fact, but here in Washington, this has been greeted thus far with relative silence, which I believe contributes to the invisibilization and isolation of immigrant communities in our midst.”

Immigration enforcement has quietly increased across the country this summer, with ICE eschewing the more dramatic “surges” it conducted earlier in the year in Minneapolis, Chicago, and other cities. Washington state has been no exception to this swell, and Godoy said she expects to see the numbers continue to rise over time.
The Seattle Times reported that 74% of ICE arrests in Washington in June and July did not involve people with criminal convictions or pending charges.

Guillermo Rivera from Eastside for All, an equity advocacy organization, spoke about the detentions being observed on the Eastside at the press conference. “Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles, and this is not only happening in East King County, this is happening all around the state,” Rivera said. “The people are being detained when they are driving. People, we are afraid now to go into our cars, that they can stop us at any time. We're afraid to go to the supermarket, to take the kids to the doctor, to take our children to school.”

The UWHRC report described a common new technique being seen in ICE detentions known as “jump outs.” “Jump outs” involve multiple unmarked vehicles, sometimes lacking license plates, surrounding a target who is driving. Unidentified officers then jump out of their cars and violently detain their target. Officers often already know the name of the person they are detaining due to the state driver data they have accessed.
The “jump out” has become one of ICE’s key enforcement strategies since President Donald Trump began his second term.

19 of 22 shootings by immigration agents in Trump’s second term have taken place during these ICE traffic stops, an analysis this summer found, with the UWHRC identifying at least two additional ICE shootings during traffic stops since then.

The increasing brutality of immigration enforcement is also typified by two recent investments by ICE: up to $2 million on robot dogs and up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks.

Meanwhile, local lawmakers still don’t know if ICE is planning to buy the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, which could stymie state efforts to impose oversight on the facility. ICE’s current contract with the facility is set to expire on October 27.

The detention center has been receiving complaints about poor and dehumanizing conditions for years. Indeed, conditions there are so bad that Washington State Senator Yasmin Trudeau (D-Tacoma) refers to the facility as a concentration camp.

UW researchers found evidence that in Minnesota, driver data queries were also being used to obtain information about community observers of ICE activity, which shows how similar tactics can be used to both increase immigration detentions and to surveil U.S. citizens without a warrant.
The UWHRC also found evidence that this practice is happening right here in King County.

This past June, community member Tony Andrews saw a suspicious vehicle in a Fred Meyer parking lot in Bellevue. Andrews had attended a constitutional observer training through Indivisible Eastside, which allowed him to identify the vehicle as possibly belonging to ICE. Even though Andrews kept his distance, the suspicious vehicle circled tightly around Andrews’ car in the parking lot.

Andrews gave his vehicle information to the UW researchers who submitted a records request. The returned records showed that his license plate had been run through Nlets on the day and time that the incident with the suspicious vehicle took place.
“For me, this was just a violation of my privacy,” Andrews told The Urbanist . “For the immigrants, these violations are life-changing. For them, it can mean family separation.”
The UWHRC report detailed four different pathways by which ICE and other federal agents are able to get state driver data:
The report emphasized that all pathways must be addressed simultaneously; otherwise ICE will simply shift to a new means of accessing the data.
In Washington state, ICE had been accessing driver data via direct access to the state DMV databases as recently as last year , but for now, that pathway appears to be closed.

DOL sold its data to 14 companies last year, including at least three who held Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts in the near past. While these contracts with DOL forbid the data brokers from selling the data for immigration enforcement purposes, one of the companies, LexisNexis, has structured at least one past contract with ICE in such a way that LexisNexis would have no ability to see how ICE has been using the data. Therefore, it is impossible to be confident that ICE cannot use the data broker pathway to access Washington state driver data.
Direct agency sharing data with ICE is illegal under the Keep Washington Working Act, although that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening anyway.
However, the primary way ICE appears to be accessing DMV data in Washington state at this time is through the Nlets queries.

Governor Bob Ferguson has said that his office’s actions of canceling ICE and DHS’s access to Nlets has resulted in blocking 100,000 attempts to use Nlets to access state data. However, the UWHRC report found that from January 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, DHS-affiliated agencies still searched the DOL database via Nlets 3,696,147 times, showing the gaping hole in the state’s data protections.

“What happens is that those arrest patrols, whether they're made of ICE, of the Border Patrol, of combined agencies, or of unknown masked men, simply log in under another agency's ORI, just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” Godoy said. “As a result, between January and June 2026, Washington DOL data itself shows that over one million searches were completed of Washington driver and vehicle data by agencies who are part of DHS.”
So far UWHRC has documented 38 unique ORIs, or passwords, affiliated with federal agencies prior to arrests by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) in Washington state.

The report did find that New York State has been successful at cutting off the Nlets channel of information via robust legislation. In New York, federal agents are now only able to search out-of-state license plates via Nlets.

Pacific Rim Solidarity Network sent a statement to be read at the press conference instead of coming to speak due to fears of retaliation. They called for Ferguson to enable more transparency and accountability when it comes to DOL data sharing.

“Legislatures take time, and our communities need an answer now. We cannot wait until the next fall to have protections for Washington residents,” Rivera said. “We're asking the governor's office to act now. We're asking the governor to review how this information is being collected, how it's been shared, find any gaps or misuse, and use his authority to protect Washington residents.”

If Ferguson continues to choose not to close these documented gaps, the state legislature can act in January to make the Keep Washington Working Act more robust. Godoy emphasized that being even more explicit about the need for a court warrant in order to access state driver data wouldn’t be sufficient.

“The state has already incorporated specific requirements that Nlets comply with Keep Washington Working or face consequences, and yet has been inexplicably reticent to enforce these very agreements,” the report reads.

Accordingly, Godoy suggested adding explicit enforcement mechanisms to the Keep Washington Working Act, including a private right of action so that those harmed by the data sharing could receive restitution and potentially obtain court injunctions ordering a halt to illegal data access.

“We need to demand that Washington take action to at least protect us in the ways that it can,” Godoy said. “There's no way for Washington to just expel ICE agents from the state. That's not going to happen. But they don't need to serve us up to them on a silver platter with all of our data to make it so easy for them, to allow them to legitimate their arrests and their campaign of fear. So I think for electeds, this is your moment.”
Godoy also praised community members who have chosen to be involved in rapid response in defense of their immigrant neighbors.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Advances First Construction Project
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A new 20-unit apartment building in the Central District is set to make history as the first new development constructed by Seattle's three-year-old Social Housing Developer (SSHD). With a unanimous vote of the SSHD board to acquire a 7,800-square-foot property on E Yesler Way Thursday night, the vision of growing Seattle's housing stock with a new type of permanently affordable homes takes another major step forward.

The parcel set to be transformed into social housing, located at 2402 E Yesler Way, comes with an extra layer of meaning for Seattle housing advocates. It currently belongs to the family of former House Speaker Frank Chopp, who passed away in 2025 after a long career advocating around housing issues in the state legislature. Chopp's widow, Nancy Long, currently controls the property.

"It's very emotional because Frank was the first lawmaker that came out and supported social housing when House Our Neighbors ran the first initiative and [he] talked to multiple people on our behalf," SSHD Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy told The Urbanist following the vote. "So this is an incredible moment. I know that he would be proud, and it was really amazing that Nancy brought the property to us because she wanted it to be either affordable or social housing."
Construction is planned to start in 2027, with the building opening to tenants in 2028. The sale price for the land was $1.2 million, McCoy said, with a total project cost of $15 million.

This new project will be the SSHD's second housing project overall, ahead of what is expected to be an accelerated pace of property acquisition. Earlier this year, the developer took over operations of the 150-unit Elara at the Market along Western Avenue after purchasing that 2018 building for $60.9 million. More than 10,000 people applied for a chance to live in the first phase of rental units that were opened up to new applications this past spring.

Dedicated funding for the SSHD comes from a 5% payroll tax on annual compensation over $1 million, approved by Seattle voters in February 2025 with the passage of Proposition 1A. Annual revenues that were projected at approximately $50 million have proven extremely conservative, with $115 million coming in during the first year of collections. Those additional resources are set to allow the developer to scale up faster than previously anticipated.

McCoy, who previously served as the Co-Executive Director with House Our Neighbors, took over as Interim CEO in January after Roberto Jimenez, the first pick to lead the SSHD, was fired by the board . A key hire after Jimenez's departure was Ginger Segel, brought on as chief real estate development officer.

Central District House, as the developer is calling the E Yesler Way project, will be built to passive house standards, McCoy said. Architect and Baugruppen evangelist Michael Eliason, a past contributor to The Urbanist , remains the developer's director of design & policy.

Though details around planned design are scant right now, we do know that there are plans to approach the site a little differently than a normal market rate developer would. Thanks to a state law passed earlier this year – House Bill 1687 – social housing developers have expanded authority to request variances from existing zoning standards, authority that had previously only applied to public housing authorities.

"We are looking to utilize our new power under the Housing Cooperation Law to try to to try to move a setback so that we can be better neighbors and not have windows going directly next to the next door neighbor," McCoy said.
McCoy brought up the fact that the social housing developer's first project will be built in a neighborhood that has seen significant upheaval in its population over the past few decades.

"We also recognize the deep tension – it's in the Central District, it has a very racist past in there, and there's still massive displacement that is happening," McCoy said. "So we are excited about using a community preference plan, a really robust affirmative marketing plan, learning from folks that have done that so successfully there."

Central District House is just the start of planned property acquisitions by the Social Housing Developer, with plans advancing for work on both new build projects and acquisitions. A project pipeline that received a board vote Thursday, contingent on the issuance of bonds that will allow the payroll tax funding currently coming in to be leveraged much further, would see six new construction projects and four acquisitions move forward through the end of 2027.

"There's so much more we're doing that isn't public yet because we have to wait for our board of directors to let us talk about them," McCoy said. "I see a lot of momentum. There will be another announcement [of] between 50 and 250 units that is going to be coming in the end of the year, beginning of next year, and much more to come."

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Two RapidRide R Line Stops Restored
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay transmitted RapidRide R Line alignment legislation to the King County Council. The R Line will travel between Rainier Beach station and downtown Seattle on Rainier Ave when it opens in 2032. In August, Metro asked the public for feedback on an initial alignment proposal . While many support the project, the planned removal of several existing Route 7 stops drew widespread criticism from Rainier Valley residents , transit advocates , and disability advocates .

In response to this feedback, the latest plan restores the stops on Rainier at Bayview St and State St/Grand St. The King County Council will discuss and vote on the R Line’s alignment over the next few weeks. This will establish the route’s path and general station locations. Additional project components, such as transit priority infrastructure, new crossings, and sidewalk improvements, will be finalized in later project stages. Executive Zahilay has proposed front-loading the project’s budget in an effort to potentially move up the R Line’s opening date.

Another key feedback theme Metro received involved the removal of stops along the Prentice Street loop. Today, every third Route 7 bus continues south of Henderson St to provide coverage in Rainier Beach. The R Line will turn right on to Henderson and terminate at the Rainier Beach Link station. In response, Metro highlighted Route 106 on Renton Ave and the Rainier Beach Metro Flex zone. The agency is also planning a southeast Seattle restructure that will take place in 2028 or 2029. Based on feedback received during restructure process, Metro may adjust other routes to back-fill Prentice St loop coverage once the R Line launches in 2032.

articles.title: Refining ramen on Capitol Hill: A decade of noodles, craft, and devotion at Ooink
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Ten years after launching their cozy Capitol Hill ramen spot above the Broadway and Pike QFC , Ooink founders Chong Boon Ooi and Jiaxin Wang are marking a decade in business.

Before establishing the shop, Malaysian-born chef Chong logged 15 years in kitchens across Los Angeles, Paris, Las Vegas, New York City, and Hawaii before choosing Seattle as the permanent home to build his craft and raise a family.

Rather than overhauling the menu to chase trends, Chong’s foundation has been meticulous refinement. As he told CHS about his culinary approach, “We still try to refine what we do and achieve better. I don’t like to create new dishes, I like to do what I do and make it better.”
The result is a noodle shop for noodle lovers. While people sometimes line up around the block for social media-driven ramen hype in the neighborhood, Ooink’s success is about devotion and longevity.

The focus has included small innovations over the years, from mala-spiced bowls to rich broths, shallot-and-goose-fat Shanghai Style Shoyu, and sourcing soft, alkaline natural spring water from a tap in Lynnwood to make his house noodles noticeably lighter and fluffier.

Ooink navigated the pandemic and industry shifts with to-go ramen kits and a hearty fried chicken sandwich, supported throughout by a devoted following. That sustained enthusiasm fueled an expansion across town, leading the team to open a second Ooink outpost at 3630 Stone Way N in Fremont.

CHS reported here on the 2016 debut of Ooink as the first-time restaurant owners were happy to take over a fully built-out space where another food and drink venture had just gone kaput. Ooink has endured, even outlasting Harvard Market ownership. Early this year, the shopping center was acquired by San Diego-based developer Tourmaline Capital for $14.2 million. Increased maintenance and more spending on security has followed and helped address some of the public safety issues on the block.
Reflecting on the decade, Ooi and Wang, have a message for Capitol HIll:

Ten years ago, we opened a tiny ramen shop above the QFC on Capitol Hill with a small menu, big dreams, and probably not enough sleep. We didn’t know how many bowls we’d serve, how many friends we’d make, or how much Seattle would become home. Ten years later, we’re still here, making noodles fresh, refining our broth, serving the ramen we believe in, and feeling incredibly grateful for every person who has slurped, sweated, waited, supported, and come back for another bowl. From our first little shop to the Ooink family today: thank you for 10 years of ramen, community, and memories.
Ooink is located at 1416 Harvard Ave. You can learn more at ooinkramen.com .

articles.title: $16.7M: Follow-up to April audit shows how King County Regional Homelessness Authority’s shortfall built over years
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Calls are growing louder to scrap the effort altogether with revelations that the King County Regional Homelessness Authority has an estimated $16.7 million “unresolved funding” shortfall on its hands and owes millions to the King County Investment Pool .
A review commissioned by the city and King County found no evidence of missing or diverted funds.

Instead, officials say the deficit stems from $15.6 million in lost administrative revenue. Under shifting local priorities and funding, and tied up in bureaucracy and process, service providers spent far less grant money than budgeted, which cut the administrative fees KCRHA was set to earn. KCRHA also spent $3.3 million beyond its funding caps on Salesforce, temporary staff, and legal fees, and racked up $2.4 million in net interest by running overdraft balances in the King County Investment Pool, a county treasury structure that manages operating funds and provides liquidity for regional public agencies.
The report (PDF) attributed the failure to weak financial management systems that failed to link budgeting, billing, and cash reconciliation.
To stabilize operations, KCRHA officials say they are rebuilding accounting controls.
In 2027, KCRHA will transfer local contract administration back to Seattle and King County, refocusing the agency on a smaller portfolio of state and federal responsibilities.

The downsizing of the authority began this summer as officials were forced to restructure the KCRHA after a troubling April 2026 forensic audit found massive deficiencies in the authority’s financial management, internal controls, and oversight.

The authority was formed as officials pledged the new effort would consolidate efforts to address the homelessness crisis at a broader, more regional level. At one point growing to a $250 million a year effort, KCRHA was officially established in late 2019 through an Interlocal Agreement between the county and the City of Seattle under then- Mayor Jenny Durkan and then- King County Executive Dow Constantine .
The King County Regional Homelessness Authority is currently led by Kelly Kinnison who has served as its Chief Executive Officer since 2024 .
The KCHRA’s budget was proposed as $205 million in 2026 with about 60% coming from Seattle and the rest from the county and state and federal pass-through grants.
Seattle is shifting its homelessness spending. Mayor Katie Wilson’s deficit-snuffing budget proposal incorporates the return of homelessness contracting to the city.

In a joint statement, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay and Wilson said the county and city are working on a repayment plan to cover the KCHRA shortfall financed on credit through King County’s treasury as the authority continues its restructuring.
Others are calling for the plug to be pulled. King County Councilmember Rod Dembowski and Seattle City Councilmember Maritza Rivera repeated calls for the authority’s dissolution.

articles.title: Slog AM: Shooter Kills Four in Bend, White Powder Mailed to Washington State Elections Office, a Stupid Flying Car
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Four dead in Bend shooting: A 16-year-old boy allegedly entered Bend, Oregon’s Silver Rail Elementary School with a long gun, opened fire, and killed three children ages 5, 8, and 11, and a teacher. Another child and another teacher were injured. A bystander saw the boy “blasting his way into the school,” followed him inside, and shot and killed him.

Shout out to our corrupt oligarchs! Amazon, Microsoft, and T-Mobile donated a collective $20 million to fund President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project. This should be all the fuel Rep. Shaun Scott needs to revive his dream of a statewide big business payroll tax.

Another one for the guillotine: A proposed class-action lawsuit alleges Expedia drove up hotel prices by “artificially inflating hotel rates by prohibiting hotels from offering lower rates elsewhere,” the Seattle Times reports . According to the lawsuit, hotels pay a fat commission to Expedia, which they recoup by raising prices. If a hotel doesn’t follow the rules, Expedia will punish it by moving it lower in search results.

It’s so 2001 again: A letter filled with an unknown white powder was sent to the Washington secretary of state’s election division. Law enforcement intercepted it before it got to its intended destination. But c’mon, please do not mail anthrax to the election workers. Or anyone, for that matter!

No contract for Washington Appellate Project: WAP, the state’s only non-profit appellate public defense law firm—one which handles 40 percent of Washington’s public defense appeals—hasn’t reached a deal for a new contract with the Washington State Office of Public Defense (OPD) and may have to close its doors by the end of the year, the Urbanist reports . Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, Washington Post photographer in West Bank: A mass coordinated attack occurred in the West Bank when dozens of black-clad, masked Israeli settlers descended upon Palestinian villagers as they were harvesting olives. They set groves ablaze and slung rocks. They also attacked veteran WaPo photographer Heidi Lavine in her clearly marked “PRESS” vest, knocking her to the ground, taking her phone and camera, and kicking her repeatedly. Public executions for people who have abortions: That’s what new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia believes in. Zacharia sat on the board up until this year.

A flying car? Elon Musk unveiled what he’s calling the world’s first flying car. Flying? Buddy, that looks more like falling with style.

Proving why it should pass: Mega-rich California residents are spending big to defeat a ballot proposition that would levy a one-time 5 percent tax on any California resident worth more than a billion dollars. The revenue generated would fund mostly health care programs, with some going toward education and food assistance. The opposition campaign has raised more than $340 million and is spending $1 million a day to defeat the proposition. Donors include “Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists,” reports the Guardian . California, you better do the right thing and make these knobs pay up. There is no such thing as an ethical billionaire and these bozos are proving it.

Matt Gaetz sued for sex trafficking: Two women filed a federal civil lawsuit against ex-Florida Congressman and former Attorney General favorite Gaetz for allegedly participating in a sex trafficking scheme “involving young women, drugs, and traveling across state lines,” reports the Miami Herald . It’s the same sex scandal that put the kibosh on his Attorney General dreams. He resigned from Congress while a bipartisan House Ethics Committee investigated his misconduct. Now, to deal with the lawsuit, Gaetz has attempted to dox the women who filed it. He posted a photo of three women in bikinis with the name of one woman, though he said later he wasn’t sure any of the women in the photo were the women suing him.

Good for them: The Milwaukee Brewers just swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series. They’re headed to their first World Series since 1982. They’ll play either the Tampa Bay Rays or the Cleveland Guardians.

paras: Join celebrated director Lynn Novick for a preview of her new landmark PBS documentary, Crime and Punishment in America, followed by a post-show discussion with Ear Hustle podcast hosts, Earlonne Woods and Nigel Poor.

The new four-part, eight-hour series, executive produced by Ken Burns and Sam Pollard, tells the consequential story of criminal justice in America as it has never before been told — from the colonial era to today. The PBS extended trailer is available here , and a first look from the film is available here .

Narrated by Keith David, Crime and Punishment in America is the first documentary project to comprehensively explore the arguments Americans have had over the problem of crime, the purpose of punishment, and the meaning of justice for more than 250 years. The film offers a sweeping look at the American criminal justice system, from the origins of prisons and policing to our continued fascination with crime, and traces the contours of our imperfect system and how it influences nearly all parts of our society: the media, economics, and politics. Through the voices and testimony of those who have committed crimes, experienced incarceration, enforced the law, or lost loved ones to violence, the series explores the cost of America’s choices and the enduring tension between crime and punishment, vengeance and mercy, justice and redemption. Crime and Punishment in America will air over four consecutive nights on PBS beginning November 16, 2026, and will stream on all PBS digital platforms for four weeks.

After sharing a curated selection of clips from the eight-hour series, Novick will sit down with the hosts of the Pulitzer finalist podcast Ear Hustle , Earlonne Woods and Nigel Poor, to discuss the film’s making and perspectives on the American carceral system.

articles.title: A look at WA’s 3rd, 4th and 5th District Congressional races
articles.author: Paris Jackson
paras: The midterm election is less than 3 weeks away. This year all voters in Washington will vote on their members of Congress, with each of the state’s 10 U.S. House Seats on the ballot.

We’re reviewing congressional races in the 3rd, 4th and 5th Districts in the state – including one that is one of the closest in the nation. Longtime Washington State Standard political reporter, Jerry Cornfield says all seats have varied political significance.
In the southwestern portion of the state, is the 3rd Congressional District. The race with the most attention, money and national implications.
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkemp Perez, a Democrat who often sides with Republicans, is clawing to keep her seat against Republican state senator and businessman, John Braun.

“When I last looked Republicans held a four-seat advantage over Democrats in the U.S. House. There's less than two dozen races around the country that are even considered competitive. This is one of them. So, the winner of this race will help determine who's going to have the majority in the U.S. House next year,” Cornfield said.
Cornfield says if this seat flipped, it would be a huge boost for Republicans.

“Washington state is heavily Democratic in its congressional delegation. So, if Senator John Braun, the Republican, is able to take the seat back, as Republicans did hold it for more than a decade prior to a Democrat Marie Glusenkemp-Perez winning, it would be a big win for the party. They've been suffering losses in the state legislative races and the congressional races, and this is one that will be a good barometer of just where is the Republican Party, at least in the southwest part of the state,” Cornfield said.

In the central part of Washington, including Yakima and the Tri-Cities, voters are weighing the open seat for District 4. Republican congressman Dan Newhouse is not seeking re-election. The race is between Republican Amanda McKinney, and Democrat John Duresky.

“Amanda McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, is running with the endorsement of President Donald Trump. And she is all-in after a recent debate, with the Trump MAGA agenda and is 100% in line with him. John Duresky has got a long history in the community... but he's not as well-funded. The Democrats are not lined up to push him through, but there is a “blue wave” that's on the East Coast, and it's making its way to the West Coast. And this is one of those races where you just wonder, are Democrats and the Independents ready to walk away and do something they haven't done in a long time, and that's elect a Democrat to this district,” Cornfield said.

The 5th Congressional district includes Spokane, the largest city in eastern Washington. This is the other seat in Washington currently held by a Republican, Michael Baumgartner, but in this case, he’s running for re-election.

“Michael Baumgartner is in his first term, and he too has the support of President Donald Trump. Carmela Conroy, the Democrat, ran against him. You know, they fought against each other two years ago on the ballot. So, it is a kind of a rematch of sorts. On paper, again, like the 4th Congressional District it looks pretty one-sided for the Republican. However, just in recent weeks, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said, ‘we think that blue wave is going to wash ashore in that district, and we can bring Carmela Conroy over to a victory and turn it from red to blue.’ I think that's a long shot,” Cornfield said.
While the 7 other races all feature a Democrat and Republican, analysts expect them all to stay in Democratic control.

articles.title: Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control
articles.author:
<name>Jillian Turanovic, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jillian-turanovic-2548303"/>
paras: A gunman shot and killed three children and a teacher at a school in Bend, Oregon , on Oct. 15, 2026, the 52nd school shooting this year , according to CNN. The children’s ages were 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The 16-year-old shooting suspect was shot and killed by a bystander.

Though Oregon has stricter gun laws than most states , some of those laws, such as a measure requiring tougher background checks and requiring a person to have a permit in order to buy a gun, are stalled in court.

The Bend shooting – the latest in a long line of modern school shootings dating back to the late 1980s – comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws.

Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to . If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.

Gun control is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been a recurring part of American life .

Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, at least two students on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at Florida State University . As one of them put it: “This is America.”

Researchers have called today’s young adults the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era , with routine lockdown drills , heightened security in schools and nonstop media coverage of mass violence .

As criminologists who study the impacts of victimization and gun violence among young people , we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In a recent study , we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.

Mass shootings account for about 1% of gun deaths in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 survey by the American Psychological Association , nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they avoided certain places because of it . The fear has become so common that clinicians now have screening tools to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.

Young adults have also grown up watching the same heated gun debates play out after every tragedy. Gun control advocates call for stricter firearm restrictions to prevent the next mass shooting , whereas gun rights advocates push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase made popular by the National Rifle Association . Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses .

Researchers have known for a long time that more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence . A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after decades of mass shootings , federal gun policy has barely budged . Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois , they’ve faced Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court .

Young people have become some of the loudest voices in this debate , most notably through March for Our Lives – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and other youth-led groups across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among older Americans , many political observers assume stricter gun laws will follow as young people gain voting power .
This fall, voters in a few states will weigh in on gun policy directly.

In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to keep or repeal a 2024 law that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to change the state constitution to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.

So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. Our survey asked young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.

In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.

We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high.

In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the largest voting bloc in the country . Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Oct. 15, 2026.

articles.title: Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less
articles.author:
<name>Vanessa M. Conzon, Assistant Professor of Management and Organizations, Boston College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/vanessa-m-conzon-2374332"/>
paras: If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise.

Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, 36% of American workers in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

I’m a management scholar who studies how, when and where people work . Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives.

The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected.

Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be published in an upcoming issue of the management journal Organization Science.

Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent researchers of workplace relationships – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong.

In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work.

For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer.

“Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office.

Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen.
In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked.

“Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work.
Psychological safety is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively.
Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including learning, creativity and speaking up .
Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers.

People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress.
After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives.
And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another.
When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together.
“I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.”

The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it.

This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.”

Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety.

My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better.

articles.title: Belonging and belief: Why evangelical churches draw many migrants in the US
articles.author:
<name>Johanna Bard Richlin, Associate Professor of Anthropology, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/johanna-bard-richlin-1481530"/>
paras: In October 2024, right before the presidential election, I had coffee with Kim, a Congolese asylum-seeker living in southern Maine. Our conversation quickly turned to politics, and I cautiously asked about her views, although she could not vote.
During his campaign, Donald Trump had vowed mass deportations , and I assumed immigration policies would be among her top priorities.

But instead, she quickly turned to matters of faith, invoking her strongly held beliefs. Kim – a pseudonym, like all names used in this article – was an evangelical Christian whose life revolved around her church: a nondenominational congregation led by other Congolese migrants.

“Democrats are not people of God,” she declared. People in her community were “traditional,” she added, and generally wanted politicians who were, too. Congolese Christians, she said, usually believed marriage should only occur between a man and a woman, that sex and gender are chosen by God, and that life is sacred from conception.

Her pronouncement underscores an important but often overlooked reality. Popular commentary in the U.S. often portrays evangelicals as one homogeneous, overwhelmingly white group. In reality, they are diverse, from political views and geography to race: 3 in 10 U.S. evangelicals are not white.
And a growing percentage are migrants – a term I use for people who have come to the U.S., regardless of their legal status.

Overall, 12% of evangelicals in the U.S. were born outside the country, according to a 2024 study conducted by the Pew Research Center. Another 7% have at least one parent born outside the country. These figures are likely underestimates, since undocumented migrants generally avoid surveys for fear of deportation.

As an anthropologist of religion , I’ve studied the growing number of migrants drawn to evangelical faith – and learned how significantly faith shapes their lives in the United States. In turn, these migrants are shaping America’s religious landscape .

While writing my 2022 book, “ In the Hands of God ,” I spent over a year attending evangelical churches around Washington, D.C., that catered to Brazilian migrants. I interviewed about 80 churchgoers and surveyed dozens more.

Congregants described how belief and belonging helped them overcome challenges such as loneliness, “feeling stuck” due to their legal precariousness and being exploited at work. I heard stories of employers holding migrants’ passports hostage, or refusing to pay construction workers seriously injured on the job.

Migrants often told me that their churches’ close-knit communities, and evangelical Christianity’s emphasis on fostering an intimate relationship with God, gave them a sense of empowerment . Through prayer, worship, Bible study and fasting, they tried to discern and implement God’s plan for their lives.

The three congregations that I attended offered multiple prayer, study and worship opportunities for migrants throughout the week, both at church and at congregants’ homes. Many pastors were migrants themselves and shared from the pulpit their stories of overcoming adversity.
Gláucia, an undocumented migrant from Brazil, described leaving herself “in the hands of God” as she faced uncertainty about her future.

“I love living here,” she explained. “But if God wants me to leave, I’m under God’s will. Wherever God directs me, I will go. Therefore, I don’t get worried, because we can’t become worried about what comes tomorrow. Because tomorrow belongs to God.
"The most I can do,” she added, “which I always try to do, is pray to God to give direction” to political leaders.

Some people I met identified as evangelical before coming to the U.S., but a significant number were converts. Even among people who had attended evangelical churches in Brazil, many insisted that they truly “met Jesus” in the United States and reflected that their faith back home had been “lukewarm.”

Angela, an undocumented migrant, knew many evangelicals in Brazil. It wasn’t until arriving in the U.S., though, that she converted from Catholicism. She told me, “When you are here, without your family, without any friends, you feel alone, and look for something to hold on to,” she told me.
According to large-scale surveys, most immigrants in the U.S. are Christian , and the majority of Christian migrants are Catholic .

Over the past several decades, however, a growing percentage of people in Latin America, long a Catholic stronghold, have been embracing evangelical churches . That has influenced the religious makeup of migrants to the United States. Others convert to evangelical Christianity once they arrive , as my research highlights.

Most of the migrants I met reported intense psychological pain as they endured family separation, workplace exploitation and legal uncertainty, which prompted them to search for meaning and comfort in religious spaces. Migrant evangelical churches, they found, spoke directly to their distress . Their style of worship and theological teachings provided concrete tools, including practices such as prayer, fasting and sharing personal testimony, that relieved migrants’ suffering.

Research suggests it is also common for migrants from other parts of the world, including Taiwan and China , to turn to evangelical, charismatic and Pentecostal churches to address difficulties they confront in the United States .

Evangelical churches play a major role in these migrants’ experiences of the U.S. In turn, these migrants are playing a significant role in American Christianity, as I explain in “ The Handbook of Contemporary Christianity in the United States .”
Over the past few decades, Americans have become less Christian and less religious . In 2007, 78% of Americans called themselves Christians; today, that number is 63%.

Migrants, however, are more likely to have a religious affiliation : 87%, compared with 70% of all people in the United States. In Maine, for example, where I live, journalists have noted how African migrants are reinvigorating churches . And many thriving migrant churches are evangelical .

Looking toward the future, I believe these trends will continue to transform U.S. religion, which may affect politics as well. Many migrants I met, including green-card holders and asylum-seekers, hoped to eventually gain citizenship and be able to vote. Many attended church alongside their own children, born in the U.S. – future voters whose attitudes may be shaped by their parents’ experiences of both migration and faith.

I learned that evangelical migrants’ identity as “people of God” was central to their political views, as it is for their white, U.S.-born counterparts. Some of them believed Trump would restore the United States to its presumed destiny as an explicitly Christian nation. His policies about abortion, marriage and gender seemed to outweigh concerns about the risks his immigration policies posed to them and their families. Since the start of his second term, with its waves of sometimes violent and aggressive ICE raids , detentions and deportations, I have wondered how they would assess the administration today.

Regardless of their political views, it is clear that migrants will continue to look to evangelical faith to cope with and make sense of their experiences in the United States. My research underscores the significant role evangelical faith plays in the life of growing numbers of migrants and the far-reaching impacts of such faith for U.S. society.

Johanna Bard Richlin does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Treating depression during pregnancy may benefit baby’s brain development – new research
articles.author:
<name>Elysia Poggi Davis, Professor of Psychology, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/elysia-poggi-davis-2760759"/>
paras: Treating pregnant women’s depression with a short course of talk therapy doesn’t just improve their health – it can also shape how their babies’ brains develop before birth . That’s the finding of a new study we co-authored, published in the journal Nature Communications.

The study is part of an ongoing research project that explores how a form of brief interpersonal psychotherapy called MOMCare, which is specially tailored to treating prenatal depression , affects pregnant women with depression and their babies. MOMCare consists of eight 50-minute sessions focused on building interpersonal skills, reducing conflict and strengthening social support.

We enrolled 234 pregnant women who reported having symptoms of depression during their routine prenatal care appointments. Mothers joined the research project during the first or second trimester and were randomly assigned to one of two groups.

Women in one group received MOMCare. Women in the other group received education about mental health, strategies for managing depression symptoms and referrals to mental health support services, such as therapy, in the community. Both groups continued getting their usual medical care, which could also include referrals to therapy or medication.

In a previous publication, we found that 36% of moms enrolled in our study were diagnosed with depression in pregnancy before getting MOMCare and just 6% after it , showing the intervention was effective. Women who received the MOMCare intervention were also more likely to carry their baby to term , which is linked with shorter hospital stays after birth and improvements in many aspects of child health and development, including better school performance .

In the current study, to investigate how this form of talk therapy affects a baby’s developing brain, we measured the volume of different brain areas using an imaging technique called magnetic resonance imaging , or MRI, within a few weeks of birth. We found that a brain area called the hippocampus , which plays a role in learning, memory and emotional regulation , was 5% smaller by volume in infants whose mothers received MOMCare compared to mothers in the other group.

Six months later, we brought the babies back into the lab to examine their emotional responses to unfamiliar experiences, such as encountering a noisy toy robot that danced and moved unpredictably. According to earlier studies, babies who respond more negatively to these tasks have higher levels of depression and anxiety in adolescence.
In our study, we found that babies with a smaller hippocampal volume at birth tended to respond less negatively than those with larger volume.

It may seem counterintuitive that a smaller brain volume is associated with stronger emotional regulation, particularly since in adults smaller brain volume is often associated with negative effects . However, in infancy the brain is growing , and faster growth may not always be advantageous. For example, one hypothesis proposes that stress can accelerate early brain development .

Depression affects up to 1 in 5 women during pregnancy . It also raises the risk of pregnancy complications such as high blood pressure and preterm birth. And having depression during pregnancy raises the risk of mental illness in the child .

Pregnancy offers a unique opportunity to simultaneously improve the health of both mother and baby. This is because women often have more contact with the healthcare system during pregnancy than at other times in their lives. Treating a woman’s depression during her pregnancy benefits two generations , improving the health of the mother and her developing baby.

Even though both MOMCare and the control condition in our study provided more support than pregnant women experiencing symptoms of depression often receive, we still saw a big difference between the groups. This suggests that a targeted intervention, even a noninvasive and relatively low-cost one such as MOMCare, can make a big difference.

Our study is the first to show that treating a woman’s depression during pregnancy may influence infant brain development. It aligns with a small but growing number of randomized clinical trials showing that reducing maternal depression has benefits for babies, including improved emotional development and changes in stress-related hormones .

These findings, if confirmed, could explain the biological underpinnings behind why treating prenatal depression is so critical. Further, they support public health initiatives to increase accessible mental health support during pregnancy.

It’s not clear how lessening mom’s depression in pregnancy leads to changes in the baby’s brain. It’s possible, for example, that stress-related hormones or inflammation associated with depression could influence brain growth.

Another open question is how the brain changes we observed might affect babies’ development long term. We hope to address this by continuing to follow mothers and babies through early childhood. By tracking conditions such as depression and anxiety as the children get older, we hope to determine whether treating mothers’ depression in pregnancy has lasting benefits for their children’s mental health and well-being.
The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.
