articles.title: Fentanyl is fueling overdose deaths in Colorado – what voters need to know about Proposition 132’s attempt to stiffen penalties
articles.author:
<name>Joshua Barocas, Professor of Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/joshua-barocas-2330479"/>
paras: Colorado continues to face an increase in overdose deaths while other states have seen a downturn.

Illicitly manufactured fentanyl, a potent opioid, emerged in the Colorado drug market around 2018. That was nearly five years after it began tormenting people who use street drugs in Northeastern states .
By 2019, fentanyl replaced other drugs as the driving force behind opioid overdoses in Colorado , and it has held its grip ever since.

But while overdose deaths in the U.S. are currently experiencing a historic decline of almost 14%, Colorado is one of eight states where rates are not dropping . In fact, Colorado has had an increase of nearly 12% in overdose deaths since April 2025.
Overdoses are top of mind for many everyday Coloradans, healthcare professionals, elected officials and public health experts like me .

Proposition 132 attempts to address these concerns by stiffening legal penalties. A conservative policy organization called Advance Colorado collected the signatures to get the initiative on the November ballot.

The proposed change to Colorado law would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony, require a mandatory minimum eight-year prison sentence for distribution of any quantity of fentanyl, and eliminate some existing opportunities for reduced penalties.
Before Coloradans head to the polls, it is worth examining the state’s overdose trends and considering whether Proposition 132 is likely to solve the problem.
Let’s start by looking at Colorado’s past attempts to stop drug overdoses through legislation.
In recent years, the state has pursued some public health interventions but has leaned heavily on increasing criminal penalties for using and possessing fentanyl.
The 2022 Fentanyl Accountability and Prevention Act (HB22-1326) , for instance, represented a major expansion of criminal penalties.

This law rolled back a 2019 law that had decriminalized small amounts of drugs. Specifically, HB22-1326 made the knowing possession of more than 1 gram and up to 4 grams of a substance containing fentanyl a Level 4 drug felony punishable by up to 180 days in jail and two years of probation.

Unlike Proposition 132, the 2022 fentanyl act directed funding for the distribution of naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, and fentanyl test strips that help people identify fentanyl in their drugs before using them. Both naloxone and fentanyl test strips decrease the risk of fatal overdose.
The law did not direct funding toward evidence-based treatments such as methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder .
Supporters argued that the legislation was necessary to prevent overdose deaths and get people treatment.

I led a research team that included addiction treatment providers and substance use–focused epidemiologists to study the effects of HB22-1326. Although more people were arrested and faced the tougher penalties, we found no increase in people beginning or staying on buprenorphine . We also found that fewer people were starting and staying on methadone following the implementation of the law.

Importantly, we found that the law did not change the trajectory of overdose deaths compared to what was expected. Taken together, we found no substantial evidence that increasing criminal penalties, even with some increased funding for naloxone and overdose prevention, “saved lives” as proponents had hoped.

Colorado is already uniquely punitive toward people who use illicit drugs , with some of the harshest penalties for drug possession and distribution in the U.S. Colorado’s public health response has developed alongside, not in place of, a substantial criminal-legal response.

Even with efforts to provide additional access to harm-reduction protections , escalating criminal penalties have not produced the treatment gains or decreases in overdose deaths in Colorado that proponents promised.
So, let’s look at a place in the state where overdose deaths are actually falling to see what is being done differently there.

Larimer County, home of Colorado State University and part of Rocky Mountain National Park, offers the clearest contrast to the rest of the state. Accidental overdose deaths have declined year after year since 2022 , down nearly 42% from 2021.
For one, the Larimer County Jail is one of less than half of the Colorado county jails that offers that includes medications for opioid use disorder.

The sheriff’s office, in collaboration with several community-based organizations, has also flooded the community with naloxone through the Reversal Project . Furthermore, using opioid abatement funds , the county has expanded youth and family support services, co-responder units and other harm-reduction services. The county has also steadily increased the number of people on buprenorphine .

No single intervention can be credited with Larimer County’s decline in accidental overdoes deaths. Criminal enforcement remains one component of the county’s response. Yet, what stands out is its emphasis on evidence-based interventions with an emphasis on expanding treatment access and harm-reduction services that save lives and give people the stability and opportunity to build healthier lives.
In addition, Proposition 132 has a major flaw. It targets one drug: fentanyl.
But the available data suggests most people take fentanyl together with stimulants such as methamphetamine. Both drugs can be fatal.
Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 40% of overdose deaths in Colorado involved both opioids and stimulants.
National figures follow a similar pattern. Nationally, 43% of overdose deaths in 2024 involved both opioids and stimulants .

Targeting one substance, as Proposition 132 does, ignores the fact that the state has a true “polysubstance” epidemic and will end up making people who unknowingly possess fentanyl susceptible to harsher penalties set forth by Proposition 132.
Since Colorado increased fentanyl penalties in 2022, the promised treatment gains examined in our research have not materialized. The state’s number of overdoses has continued to climb.

Those facts do not mean that criminal penalties alone caused Colorado’s worsening trend. But they do raise an important question as voters consider Proposition 132: What evidence suggests that increasing those penalties further will address the rise in overdose deaths?
Joshua Barocas receives funding from the National Institutes on Drug Abuse and has previously received funding from the Colorado Department of Human Services.

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
articles.author:
<name>Jaquelyn Jahn, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology, Drexel University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jaquelyn-jahn-2768054"/>
paras: When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons.

Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project , “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.”

I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people . My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years.

While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons.

Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme . Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs , Dallas , Laurel Highlands , Muncy , Waymart and Huntingdon , the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country , those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.

Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease , and the state’s prison population is getting older , which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023 .
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year . That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults.

The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time , because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.

Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs . But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers.

In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour .

One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men.

This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.

Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “ accelerated aging ” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected.
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable.

Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.

articles.title: Amazon’s NBA coverage adds Prime 360 — AI replays that ‘fly the camera through’ the action
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon is bringing a new AI-powered camera system to the court as the tech giant gets ready to tip off its second season of basketball coverage on Prime Video.

Called Prime 360, the technology uses an array of high-resolution cameras positioned around the arena to capture plays from multiple angles. Amazon’s proprietary AI models then process the footage to create highlight replays that the company says traditional cameras can’t replicate.

The feature will appear during live games and as an analysis tool on the pregame, halftime and postgame shows for select broadcasts. Amazon said it built the system with a team of producers, engineers and AI scientists, using its in-house AWS Trainium chips.
“Think of it like a video game camera,” Josh Green, an associate producer, said in an Amazon video describing the tech (below).
The cameras are calibrated and synchronized, and their footage is sent to the AWS cloud, where each play is reconstructed as a 3D scene — opening up possibilities beyond a normal replay.

“I want to see this play again, and you could actually fly the camera through the play,” said Wade Wakashige, a director of product. The view gives fans at home “something that the customer in the arena can’t see,” he added.

Prime Video is also adding a fantasy basketball integration with Yahoo Sports. Viewers who link their accounts will see their fantasy rosters and real-time stats on screen during games. They’ll also get recommendations for live and upcoming games featuring players on their teams.

Amazon debuted “NBA on Prime” last October with a Celtics-Knicks game — reviewed by GeekWire — the first under an 11-year deal that gives the company exclusive rights to select regular-season and playoff games. Bloomberg reported that Amazon is paying about $1.8 billion annually for the rights.

This season, Amazon says it will stream more than 100 regular-season and postseason games. In the playoffs, that includes the Play-In Tournament exclusively, select first- and second-round games, and, for the first time, exclusive coverage of the Eastern Conference Finals.

Several tech-driven extras from the first season are back. Fans can again track their active FanDuel bets during broadcasts, though they still can’t place wagers through Prime Video. The Prime Vision alternate stream returns as well, serving as a testing ground for AI-powered stats and graphics, such as flagging offensive players in position to score, that can graduate to the main broadcast.

The “NBA on Prime” season opener is Oct. 23, with a doubleheader: the defending champion New York Knicks host the Boston Celtics at 4 p.m. PT, followed by the Houston Rockets against the San Antonio Spurs in Austin at 6:30 p.m. PT.
The programming is included with a Prime membership , which costs $139 a year or $14.99 a month. Games stream in English and Spanish on the Prime Video app and the web.

articles.title: A two-person Seattle startup lands $1M to reinvent energy-hungry chips suitable for space
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle-based TriMagnetix has landed new funding and commitments totaling $1 million to continue developing a semiconductor chip that, according to initial lab testing, consumes 800 times less energy than a traditional chip to process the same amount of data.

The startup uses nanomagnetic technology that requires only electrical pulses rather than the constant power stream traditional chips need, dramatically reducing electricity consumption and heat generation. The design also makes the chip resistant to radiation, and it’s built to integrate with existing computing infrastructure.
The startup has made additional progress beyond the new funding:
Earthbound data centers struggling to curb energy use and heat output are seeking more sustainable chips, but the startup is particularly interested in satellite applications.
The Pacific Northwest, home to companies including Starcloud and SpaceX, is the “satellite capital of the world,” said Lucas Hahn , co-founder, president and chief strategic officer of TriMagnetix.
Satellite companies have told him they want semiconductors that are energy efficient and resistant to the radiation experienced in space, Hahn said. That makes TriMagnetix’s devices “a no-brainer.”

In addition to Hahn, the startup’s other employee is Madison Hanberry , who launched the TriMagnetix in 2023. Hanberry, who has served as chief of research and development, is transitioning to CEO. His sister, Aspen White , is also a co-founder.

The chips made so far by TriMagnetix are not the high-performance graphics processing units, or GPUs, used for applications such as AI and 3D animation. Nor are they simpler central processing units, or CPUs.
“It’s replacing specific compute in certain devices at a very low level,” Hahn said. “So not quite CPU yet, but it is at the core level doing similar things.”

TriMagnetix has contracted with the Washington Nanofabrication Facility at the University of Washington to use the site’s fabrication equipment. It aims to have a product available for commercial sales within the next year.

The round was led by Acequia Capital with participation from Athenaeum Ventures . Actuate Ventures has also committed to the round. The combined total from the three firms is $1 million. Last year, the startup received a $200,000 investment from climate venture fund SNØCAP .

articles.title: Leaked list shows what Microsoft, Amazon and other tech giants are giving for the White House ballroom
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft committed $10 million to President Trump’s White House ballroom project, and Amazon and T-Mobile each chipped in $5 million, according to an internal donor list obtained by the Washington Post and reported by the newspaper Thursday morning .

The commitments are drawing scrutiny because the ballroom donations aren’t subject to campaign finance limits or disclosure requirements. The money goes through a nonprofit, the Trust for the National Mall, into a White House account the president directly controls.

Of the $333 million raised so far, the vast majority came from companies and wealthy people with interests before the federal government, the Post found, raising concerns among experts that companies could be buying influence with the administration, or feeling pressured to give.

The White House publicly named Microsoft, Amazon and T-Mobile among the ballroom’s donors last October but didn’t disclose the amounts. Other donors asked to keep their names out of it entirely, the Post found, including a subsidiary of mortgage lender Rocket, which committed $10 million weeks after a federal agency approved its acquisition of Mr. Cooper.

The Seattle-area companies have a wide range of dealings with the government as suppliers, regulated businesses and targets of federal scrutiny. Microsoft and Amazon are two of the federal government’s largest technology providers, and T-Mobile requires regulatory approval across its business, from wireless spectrum to acquisitions.

Amazon is facing an FTC antitrust trial next year, focused on its treatment of third-party sellers on its online marketplace. The FTC and 22 states also sued Amazon in August, accusing it of rigging ad auctions to overcharge advertisers.

Microsoft is at odds with Vice President JD Vance and the Labor Department over claims that the company laid off American workers while sponsoring foreign workers for permanent residency, leading the department to suspend the company from the program .

Apple and Nvidia were among the top contributors at $25 million each, according to the list of 67 donations above $10,000. Microsoft’s $10 million puts it in the next tier with Palantir and Lockheed Martin, while Amazon and T-Mobile joined Meta, Cisco and ServiceNow at $5 million.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told the Post that the donors are “a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People’s House better for generations to come.”
A Microsoft spokesperson said the company didn’t have a comment beyond what has been publicly reported. We’ve contacted Amazon and T-Mobile for comment.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Brad Smith pushes back on Vice President JD Vance’s visa fraud accusations
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft President Brad Smith says someone apparently “failed to inform the vice president accurately about our numbers” before the Trump administration cut off the company’s ability to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.

In an interview with Politico , published Thursday, Smith rejected Vice President JD Vance’s accusations of fraud and called his claim that Microsoft replaced laid-off Americans with foreign workers “completely off base.” He said Microsoft has “always been committed to a high integrity and high compliance” approach to immigration.
“We will stand by our record,” Smith said. “And I hope that folks at the White House might look again and look at what we think is a more accurate picture.”
At a White House news conference last week, Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said, after asserting that there “has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.”

Critics of the visa programs say tech companies have used them to displace U.S. workers, and that the job ads companies must run before sponsoring workers for green cards often appear in places few American job seekers will see. Labor Department records show Microsoft’s required print ads ran mostly in The Seattle Times.

Smith said most of Microsoft’s recent visa and green card applications were for people already working at the company, many of them for years, because of long green card backlogs. He also said Microsoft hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year, a number he said was “left out of the narrative.”

The Microsoft executive also rejected the idea that the company pays visa holders less. “It doesn’t matter whether you came on a visa or you’re an American worker,” he said. “Everybody has the same compensation system.”

He warned that the crackdown could send “the most talented next wave” of engineers to other countries. Five of the six tech leaders President Trump honored with national medals last week, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella , came to the U.S. as immigrants, Smith noted, and their companies together account for more than 25% of the value of the S&P 500.
The suspension doesn’t stop Microsoft from hiring foreign workers on H-1B visas. Those are temporary work visas, typically granted for three years at a time and generally limited to six.

Amazon led in H-1B approvals for new employment in fiscal 2025, with 4,644, followed by Meta with 1,555 and Microsoft with 1,394, according to an analysis of USCIS data by the National Foundation for American Policy.

What Microsoft lost is access to a key step toward permanent residency. The program, known as PERM , is run by the Labor Department. Companies use it to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency, also known as a green card. The employer has to advertise the job and show the department that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it.
PERM is commonly used for employees already working in the U.S. on temporary visas, including H-1Bs.

The interview didn’t address Microsoft’s outsized use of PERM. The company had more PERM cases decided than any other employer in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026, according to a GeekWire analysis of Labor Department data. Other big tech companies, including Amazon and Google, sharply reduced their PERM filings after early 2023.

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Zeacon aims to turn website visitors into buyers with AI-powered video
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Businesses spend heavily to attract visitors to their websites, but traffic doesn’t necessarily translate into sales. Bellevue, Wash.-based Zeacon is building AI tools to help companies connect their marketing content with customer behavior and understand what actually drives conversions.

Co-founded by Kris Naidu and Jay Gounder , Zeacon uses AI to generate videos, personalize website content and track how visitors interact with it. The platform is also designed to identify bot traffic and analyze how both people and AI agents navigate websites — an increasingly important capability as AI changes how people discover and interact with businesses online.

Zeacon’s goal is to help companies move beyond traffic and content creation to understand what turns visitors into customers. As Naidu and Gounder see it, the real measure of success isn’t how many visitors a website attracts, but how many convert.
We caught up with Kris Naidu for our latest Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your elevator pitch :

We help businesses deploy AI agents that optimize their entire digital funnel, with an initial focus on video. Our AI agents can autonomously generate video content without prompting, publish it across social media and websites, personalize the experience for each website visitor and identify bots, while continuously analyze and optimize performance.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

We are obsessed with helping businesses turn the attention they already paid for into sales. Brands invest in advertising and great video content, but the website where customers actually buy often doesn’t connect with those investments. Zeacon brings that content onto the website, personalizes it to the visitor, and connects engagement to buying behavior. We can also create new videos from product photos and website data based on what converts. The question driving us is simple: How can we help this business sell more while taking work off its team?
What surprised you after talking to customers?

How much opportunity exists in what they already have. Businesses have videos, product photos, website traffic, and customer data. What’s missing is the connection between them. A marketing team wants to know: Which content helps people buy? Where are we losing customers? What should we create next? That reinforced our belief that the real value is turning information into a decision they can act on which we can provide with our platform.
How has artificial intelligence changed the way you build your company?

AI changed what we could take off the customer’s plate. Zeacon can understand website and product information, generate video from pictures without prompting, choose relevant content for a visitor, and help teams ask questions about performance in plain English. We’re building those capabilities together: create, personalize, measure, and learn. Each result can inform the next decision. That’s a much bigger opportunity than making content faster which we can also do but it means helping a business continuously improve how it sells.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That revenue alone does not tell you how valuable an AI company is. Revenue matters it proves customers will pay. But data deserves equal attention because it determines what the system can learn and how useful it becomes. At Zeacon, we care about the connection between visitor behavior, content, and conversion. The advantage comes from the quality of that data and our ability to turn it into better customer outcomes. Investors should ask what a company is learning with every deployment, alongside what it earns that will help them understand the true growth value. Upfront value without long term vision effects companies and we were always focused on the end goal which was delivering a product that adds value not only in the near term but cannot be easily replaced.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Deciding what to say no to. When your technology opens up several opportunities, it’s tempting to pursue all of them. But customers need you to solve their problem well. Our focus is helping businesses use video and data to improve their website experience and grow sales. We have to judge opportunities against that purpose, even when they’re exciting. The data helped us understand the entire flow of users for our customers that when we had our moment. We realized it just was not about providing outcomes for sales but helping the customers fix issues within their website journey and using the content to help fill gaps for the desired outcomes.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Focus. Get close to your customers, understand the problem they will pay you to solve, and keep delivering against it. Do not confuse more features with more value. Make something customers use, trust, and want to keep. It is hard but being focused is the key to winning.
Zeacon is recognized for creating a new business science on relating content and user behavior to actual business outcomes.

articles.title: Despite Pushback, Updated RapidRide R Plans Include Scant Changes
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Updated plans for the future RapidRide R bus line between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach released this week include only a few changes to previous iterations of the project, with significant stop consolidation still planned along much of the eight-mile route despite community concerns.

The next RapidRide line to enter planning in Seattle, the R Line is set to replace the Route 7 along Rainier Avenue S by 2032, bringing upgrades to the Metro's second busiest bus line. Compared to an initial proposal put forward this summer , two stop pairs have been added for both northbound and southbound riders, including retained stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Walker Street and a new set of stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Grand Street. That change will help riders between Sound Transit's light rail stations at Judkins Park and Mount Baker more easily access bus stops, but riders further north or south could see longer walks to catch a frequent bus that is currently within easy reach.

If this plan is approved by the King County Council next month, the R Line will move forward with some major stops currently used by Route 7 riders not on the list, including 12th Ave S and Boren Ave S, Rainier Ave S and S Charles Street, and Rainier Ave S and S Andover Street. But the two stops between Judkins Park and Mount Baker do represent a response to community concerns about losing transit access along that specific stretch.

"The alignment proposal adds station pairs at Rainier Ave S & S Grand St and at Rainier Ave S & S Bayview St in response to updated ridership, new housing, community destinations, and public feedback, and retains the station pair at Rainier Ave S & S Walker St to serve nearby schools, the Lighthouse for the Blind, and riders affected by steep grades and difficult crossings," Metro's updated engagement summary notes. "Additionally, as design progresses, exact station locations will be determined by multiple conditions, including ongoing analysis and engagement."

The R Line has emerged as a major priority for King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, a bus line that connects neighborhoods across the council district he represented from 2020 to 2024. Before Zahilay took office, the R Line's budget was slashed by 25% in response to budget pressures at Metro, with a new total budget of $91.2 million.

Unlike most recent RapidRide lines including the under-construction I and J and Lines, King County does not plan to pursue federal matching funds , a fact that speaks to the current transit funding environment in D.C. But not being tethered to a USDOT grant agreement could potentially allow the County to move more quickly toward construction or implement upgrades in stages.

In releasing his biggest budget update since taking office last month, Zahilay proposed to advance $64.4 million in RapidRide R funding to the current two-year budget, in a move his office framed as intended to "build a strong partnership" with the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), also planning roadway improvements along Rainier Avenue S that are set to be implemented in the early 2030s.

""Our South Seattle communities deserve fast, reliable transit service. Residents have been waiting over a decade for the RapidRide R Line, and we are moving with urgency to deliver on this generational investment that will greatly enhance mobility while also making critical safety upgrades,” Zahilay said in an announcement of the updated plan Thursday. “During Metro’s community engagement over the summer, we heard directly from seniors, people with disabilities, and families who were concerned about losing stops along Route 7. In response to that feedback, the alignment plan proposes two additional stops. We know this will be a change for neighbors who have relied on Route 7 for years, and we will continue listening to community and working to ensure the R line meets the diverse needs of residents and riders in the Southend.”

With fewer stops to make, the R Line will move more quickly along its route, on top of planned transit speed and reliability investments including transit signal priority (TSP) and additional bus-only lanes on top of the stretches already in place. But expected time savings data for a trip on the future R Line still has not been released by Metro, a key ask of transit advocates trying to weigh the trade-offs that come with stop consolidation.

Long stretches of bus lanes that had been envisioned when the R Line entered planning nearly a decade ago are now fully implemented , including a long stretch of northbound Rainier Avenue between S Edmunds Street in Columbia City and S Grand Street just south of I-90. But Metro and SDOT have not announced any plans for transit priority along S Jackson Street, one of the current Route 7's biggest pain points.

"The Rainier Valley stop consolidation decision-making was done with data that is now fairly out of date," a September 15 letter from the advocacy group Rainier Valley Safe Streets stated. "New studies that take into account current and future ridership enabled by the large apartment complexes that have been completed since the previous studies should be done. We recognize that stop consolidation is a difficult thing to get right, but densification of the Rainier Valley, especially near Judkins Park might justify decreased stop spacing."

Metro leaders – and County Councilmembers – are likely to face a push to consider restoring even more stop pairs along the corridor, given gaps of up to a half-mile that would be created. Even in an official letter of support included in the proposal transmitted to the King County Council, Seattle's Transit Riders Union (TRU) voiced concerns that the two new stop pairs weren't enough to mitigate impacts.

"We appreciate that Metro took community feedback into account and added back additional stops between Judkins Station and Mt Baker," the letter from TRU's bus and transit subcommittee noted. "We are still concerned by the large gaps created by consolidation which effectively choose to convert this route from its current attempt to be both a local and long distance service into an express bus skipping past parts of the south end. We would like to see this project go to further planning with wiggle room on which stops to move and remove."

It also remains to be seen how Metro will address riders south of S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, along the so-called "Prentice Loop" only served by select Route 7 trips now. That area is currently served by Metro Flex microtransit service, an option that fills in the gaps in Metro's network but is absolutely not a replacement for fixed-route transit.

"Community members emphasized that the Prentice Loop and related neighborhood connections in the Rainier View and lower Rainier neighborhoods are essential for reaching schools, grocery stores, clinics, youth programs, religious centers, parks, and everyday destinations not located directly on Rainier Avenue S," the engagement summary stated. "Riders shared that existing local service helps seniors, riders with disabilities, youth, caregivers, and families access places that would otherwise require long and steep walks."
Thursday's announcement included some additional details about the future of transit service throughout broader Rainier Beach.

"Metro is also evaluating how to maintain strong and convenient transit connections for people traveling to and from areas south of South Henderson Street that will not be directly served by RapidRide R Line," the statement read, referencing potential changes to the Route 106, 107, and the 9. "Before the RapidRide R Line launches, Metro will engage communities south of South Henderson Street to better understand local travel needs, priorities, and important destinations and connections."

Even though a vote to sign off on the planned stop locations is planned for next month, the County Council will not actually be required to sign off on any adjustments to the R Line's stops, with the proposed ordinance only set to require notification.

"Before the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the executive shall notify the King County council and the city of Seattle of any substantial changes to station locations," the draft ordinance states. "Following the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the Metro transit department shall consult with the city of Seattle before making any changes to the routing or station locations."
After that vote, the R Line will advance into the next stage of planning, where Metro will align route upgrades with the project's reduced budget.

"Specific scope changes haven’t been finalized yet," Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist last month . "Those decisions will come in the next phase of design, after we confirm the route and stop locations. Once that foundation is set, we’ll be able to evaluate which capital improvements provide the greatest benefit within the appropriated budget and make informed decisions about what to carry forward into design."

articles.title: 'Unfathomable Disaster' Looms Following Public Defender Pay Dispute
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: After being unable to reach a contract agreement with the Washington State Department of Public Defense (OPD), the venerable Washington Appellate Project (WAP) may have to close its doors at the end of the year. Should this happen, the state’s court system could be disrupted due to the loss of experienced attorneys, a backlog of cases, and a more discouraging landscape for new lawyers who are considering pursuing appellate public defense.

Founded in 1993, WAP is the state’s only non-profit appellate public defense law firm and has historically handled about 40% of public defense appeals in the state: that is, appeals brought by clients who can’t afford to pay their own attorneys.

WAP attorneys have argued many life-altering cases over the years, including State v. Blake in 2021, in which the Washington state Supreme Court found the law criminalizing drug possession to be unconstitutional, and State v. Gregory in 2018, in which the Court found the death penalty in the state to be unconstitutional because it was being applied in an arbitrary and racially biased manner. They also argued a case that became part of the Miller fix that reformed how people who committed crimes as juveniles are sentenced and given a chance at parole.
Those cases illustrate how appellate public defense has the ability to impact a large number of Washingtonians by winning a single case.

“When you make the systemic changes, and I think Blake is a great example of this, it didn't just affect our client, Miss Blake,” Greg Link, the executive director of WAP, told The Urbanist . “It affected literally hundreds of thousands of people who would never be our client or never could have been our client.”
However, WAP’s contract with the state expired at the end of June, and OPD and WAP have been unable to agree on a new contract, a dispute that has ultimately led to a lawsuit.
WAP has said that the contract offered to them began a new pay model that was both unethical and unsustainable for the firm.

“OPD is currently paying WAP at rates that are unsustainable for the organization and incompatible with the amount of work required to provide effective, ethical, quality representation,” WAP wrote in their filing. “OPD also refuses to negotiate with WAP in good faith regarding appropriate compensation and case weighting designations going forward. Instead, OPD is insisting on WAP's acceptance of contractual terms that would cause WAP's attorneys to violate their constitutional and professional obligations to clients. This includes a case weighting model that provides far less time per case than a recent OPD-funded workload study deemed necessary for effective, ethical, quality appellate representation.”

OPD, on the other hand, says they are meeting the new caseload standards for public defense issued by the state Supreme Court and that the other law firms with whom they contract are able to make the new contracts work.

“First of all, we have always tied our contracts between compensation and number of cases. That has always been the case in the past, and that is the case in the current situation as well,” Katrin Johnson, the deputy director for operations at OPD, told The Urbanist . “What did change is simply that we added language to ensure greater accountability.”
The new language allows OPD greater flexibility in reassigning a case to a different firm if the original firm is unable to begin work on it.
“What's new was that language about making adjustments, if mid-year, it's clear that the contractor lacks capacity,” Johnson explained.
Link said that where WAP disagrees isn’t with the number of cases being handled by one attorney, but rather about how each case is weighted, which determines how many hours can be used on that case.

The calculation for determining case weight has changed in the most recent OPD contracts. In the past, case weight was determined by counting trial transcript pages, with one credit equaling 800 pages. With the new caseload standards, case weight is factored by counting both transcript pages and clerks’ pages, but a credit now equals 1,000 pages.
However, the disagreement over case weight calculations appears to be more fundamental than this change.
“There’s no way to tell if a case will be straightforward or all-consuming,” said Austin Field, the elections chair for the public defense chapter of SEIU 925.
The OPD contract does contain provisions offering extraordinary compensation for case outliers that require more work, for which attorneys have to apply on a case-by-case basis.

Some more complicated appellate cases can only be handled by attorneys with more experience. Link said OPD hadn’t been regulating the type of cases it was sending to WAP in this regard, creating capacity issues for the firm.
“The issue boils down to this: the Washington Appellate Project wanted a contract where they would be paid at the full time amount, yet only do half of the number of cases,” Johnson said.
Link emphasized that the structure of the new contracts is inherently creating ethical conundrums for attorneys.

“The dispute is about more than just the numbers in a contract,” Link said. “The dispute is about how public defense for people on appeal is going to be delivered. It’s about some of the terms in the contract that create [...] an incentive for attorneys to really minimize the work on any given case in order to make the maximum amount of money, the sort of things that we really don't want in public defense.”
Six law professors in the state who teach legal ethics wrote a letter supporting WAP. The Washington Defender Association also support WAP’s position .

According to Johnson, WAP filed their lawsuit against OPD while the two parties were in the middle of negotiating a six-month interim contract. More recently, WAP and OPD failed to reach a resolution through mediation, and in early September, certain claims of the lawsuit were dismissed while others continue to be in play.
The remaining lawsuit centers on WAP seeking adequate funding for their continued representation of what they say is nearly 500 people.

Without receiving more funding for its work, WAP will have to close its doors by the end of the year, meaning its remaining clients will be left without attorneys mid-case. While Washington’s public defense system is already considered to be in crisis , an additional backlog created by WAP’s current cases could worsen an already difficult situation.

“OPD has no demonstrated capacity to assign new attorneys to these individuals any time soon,” Link said. “So the crisis that looms is that come January hundreds of people will be without the attorney they are constitutionally entitled to.”
When a new attorney comes onto a case, it generally adds several months to its timeline, according to Field.
In contrast, Johnson said that recruitment for public defense appellate attorneys has been going well.

“Because the Supreme Court had lowered those caseload standards, we had to do strong recruiting of additional contract attorneys for appellate work because mathematically, if the number of cases per attorney is lower, then you need more attorneys to handle the workload,” Johnson said. “And so, in the springtime, while we were having challenges with Washington Appellate Project, we were also, meanwhile, recruiting for additional attorneys because of the reduced caseload standard. What we found was many public defenders who were at that time in trial level practice who wanted to branch into and begin doing appellate work, and the number of talented attorneys wanting to join our program was surprisingly bigger than we expected.”

While OPD is providing free training on appellate practice as well as a resource attorney to meet regularly with new appellate attorneys, the decades of appellate experience housed within WAP won’t be easy to replace, especially since only more experienced attorneys are allowed to handle more serious cases.
Field told The Urbanist that if WAP closes its doors, it would be an “unfathomable disaster.”
“It’s impossible to overstate the importance of appellate public defense,” Field said.

Appellate public defense offers opportunities to reshape the law on a structural level. And experience is critical for achieving wins with big impacts like Blake and Gregory, Link said, pointing out that it took many years before WAP was able to achieve such results.

“The one thing appeals can do is, and this is true to a very lesser degree in trial court, but appellate courts have the ability to shape the law,” Link said. “They have the ability to say this is what the law actually means, and this is what the law actually allows, in a way that's just not possible anywhere else.”

As a trial public defender himself, Field said he relies on the work of appellate public defenders to do his own work. And with WAP’s critical mass of lawyers experienced in appellate work who can collaborate on and check each other’s work while training the next generation, WAP has worked on a lot of the cases Field depends on to defend his clients today. Field thinks the loss of WAP would have wide-reaching ramifications to the quality of justice indigent people in Washington receive.

“We’re not going to be able to rely on the kind of high quality appellate advocacy that has resulted in the life-changing decisions like Blake, like Gregory, that allow us to advocate effectively at the trial court level,” Field said. “The flow of those decisions will be disrupted and we will probably see fewer critical cases like that that made such a huge difference at our level.”

Field also worries that if WAP closes its doors, new lawyers might be discouraged from pursuing public defense appellate law. Combined with the Washington state legislature’s decision earlier this year not to dedicate some of the new revenue from the millionaires tax to public defense, attorneys might not want to practice in an area of law that it appears the state’s leadership doesn’t value.
Meanwhile, the legal staff at WAP face an uncertain future.

“These are talented lawyers, paralegals, legal assistants who are dedicated to public defense,” Johnson said. “We are very concerned about their future ability to work being so impacted by their director's decision on accountability.”

The next court hearing of the WAP suit will be on Friday, November 6, when the court is set to consider dispositive motions. If the judge grants either side’s summary judgment motion, the case will most likely come to an end.

articles.title: The loading dock that saved the Madison Valley PCC
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Thanks to a PCC neighbor for the pictures

The Madison Valley PCC grocery store opened this week. As CHS reported in April , the project was a decade in the making as some neighbors fought tooth and nail after beloved neighborhood garden shop City People’s sold off its property for redevelopment.

With the co-operative market this week finally serving its first customers beneath the 82 units of The Arbory apartment building, PCC is watching how some of the compromises required to push the development over the wall of Seattle process are playing out along E Madison.
The multi-year saga over the former City People’s site on E Madison pitted neighborhood coalition Save Madison Valley against developer Velmeir and its anchor tenant.

Even before the drawn out environmental appeal, neighborhood demands and the East Design Review Board chiseled away at the project. The biggest complaints settled on the building’s mass and its relation to the single family-style homes below the Madison slope on the backside of the project but neighbors also took issue with parking and traffic plans, tree loss, and, yes, even the project’s geological engineering.
While opponents demanded reductions across the board, the core metrics held.

The architectural firm on the project responded to the complaints and board guidance with a plan that maintained the planned 25,000-square-foot footprint for the grocery. Residential density increased from an initial estimate of 75 homes to 82 units. Instead of shrinking the building, the developer redistributed mass away from the single-family zone, stepping back upper floors and adding two-story townhome walk-ups and dense landscape buffers along Dewey Place.
Early proposals featured an exposed, outdoor loading bay, drawing protests over morning diesel noise, backup alarms, and the prospect of tractor-trailers navigating residential side streets.

To secure approval from the East Design Review Board and resolve environmental appeals, the development team altered the ground-floor floor plan. They brought the loading facilities inside the building envelope along E Madison, using interior space for a buffered dock and binding delivery freight to the Madison arterial.

Enclosing the freight bay allowed the project to retain the square footage PCC required for a full-service grocery store while addressing key livability objections from neighbors and the design board. Combined with split garage access sending customer traffic and delivery trucks to Madison while directing residential parking to Dewey Place, relocating and enclosing the loading dock served as a key design concession that carried the project through city review and appeals.

Those paperwork logistics are now reality. PCC Madison Valley deliveries must follow scheduled arrival windows using smaller single-axle or straight-body rigs that can pull straight into the enclosed bay, close the roll-up door, and unload — hopefully without staging or blocking traffic on the street. Thursday afternoon, a white box truck apparently early or late ended up parked along the curb outside the store.
The grocery is the 17th location for PCC, the largest consumer-owned food cooperative in the United States with more than 125,000 members.

The 73-year-old retailer says the new store offers organic produce, ethically sourced meat and seafood, house-made sushi, a prepared-foods deli, and an updated pizza program featuring organic flour from Skagit Valley’s Cairnspring Mills . According to the co-op, product selections emphasize organic farming, animal welfare, and fair labor standards, alongside lower-priced staples through bulk goods and store-brand items.
Seattle City Council President Joy Hollingsworth , whose District 3 includes Madison Valley, praised the store’s opening in a statement released by the co-op.

“As a multi-generational Seattleite, I’m proud to support a local, homegrown business that reflects the values of our community,” Hollingsworth said. “As a farmer who runs a family-owned farm, I deeply appreciate PCC’s commitment to supporting local agriculture. And as a city official, I recognize PCC not only as a valued employer and economic driver in our region, but as a true community partner, leading on issues from hunger relief advocacy to environmental sustainability.”
PCC reports that the location employs roughly 75 unionized staff members.

Prior to opening, the co-op says it engaged with neighborhood groups, including the Madison Valley Merchants Association, Café Flora , and local schools, and backed a community push for a pedestrian crosswalk signal on E Madison.

PCC also is extending partnerships with local social service and food organizations, including the Jewish Family Service of Seattle, Bailey-Boushay House, FEEST, the Downtown Emergency Service Center, The Food Bank @ St. Mary’s, and the Black Farmers Collective .
PCC Community Markets #22 Madison Valley is located at 2925 E Madison. Learn more at pccmarkets.com .

articles.title: Man convicted in Capitol Hill fake taxi assaults faces life sentence for South Park rape
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A serial predator previously convicted of luring women into his vehicle from Capitol Hill now faces life in prison without parole following a violent abduction and rape in South Park.
King County prosecutors charged Orhan Najaar, 58, with first-degree kidnapping and second-degree rape on Tuesday, citing a pattern of posing as a driver to abduct and assault women.
KING 5 reported here on the charges and report Najaar was ordered held on $2 million bail.

Prosecutors say the latest attack occurred in November 2024, just weeks after Najaar’s release from prison, when he allegedly forced an injured woman into his car at knifepoint, drove her to her apartment, and repeatedly assaulted and beat her. A tool bag left behind linked the suspect to the crime.
Prosecutors say the assault mirrors Najaar’s prior predatory offenses on Capitol Hill, which qualify the case as his potential third strike under Washington law.

In 2008, Najaar posed as a cab driver outside a Capitol Hill bar, abducting an intoxicated woman and raping her before she escaped in his car. In August 2012, he offered another woman a ride home from Capitol Hill, held her captive at his residence, and raped her, eventually serving prison time after fleeing to Austria and facing extradition.

articles.title: 7 stories on 12th Ave, 10 on the Starbucks Roastery site, and now the neighborhood Goodwill — This developer has big plans for Capitol Hill apartment projects
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A massing rendering for the Goodwill site (Image: PCP)

Another sign of thawing conditions for Seattle’s development freeze could be happening on Belmont Ave E where the building and parking lot home to the neighborhood’s Goodwill has been sold for $13 million to a developer holding a massive chunk of Capitol Hill’s future in its hands.
For now, the store remains open and serving the neighborhood where it opened in spring 2014 and replaced what had been Half Price Books .

This week’s sale puts the property in the hands of PCP , an Ohio-based development firm that typically specializes in build and hold, mixed-use developments focused on up-market amenities and finishes. In recent years, PCP has aggressively pushed outside the Rust Belt into Western mountain and Pacific Northwest markets.
On Capitol Hill, the company is positioning itself as a key driver in the neighborhood’s next wave of redevelopment.
PCP’s Capitol Hill holdings include 1208 E Olive where the 12th Ave property formerly to the Car Tender auto business has been cleared for eventual development of this 7-story project .
The massing concept for the company’s planned Starbucks Roastery redevelopment (Image: PCP)

PCP’s Capitol Hill crown jewel project could come on an even more high profile site. The company touts a plan for a 10-story mixed-use project on the site of the former Starbucks Roastery at Pike and Melrose as part of its Seattle portfolio.

The not-yet-public project has no filings with the city but PCP describes it as a “10 story multifamily development in the heart of Seattle’s Capitol Hill neighborhood” planned for 174 units across a 115,000-square-foot building “with over 10,000 SF of amenity space.”

Any sale agreement or contract related to the site is also not yet public. The county still records the 1920-era building and property as remaining in the hands of its longtime ownership, Weiss-Jenkins Properties .

In commercial real estate and private development pipelines, it is common practice for firms to list properties on their website under “Pipeline” or “Land” long before any deed transfer or city permit appears in public records.
Coffee giant Starbucks abruptly shuttered the showcase roastery in September 2025 . The building has remained empty since.

Goodwill’s Belmont store will be open and bustling this Thursday but change is coming. Six years ago, CHS reported on early planning for a mixed-use project for the site and preparation for a sale of the property. Those plans have grown.

PCP says it plans to develop the project as a 22,551-square-foot site that will demolish the old Goodwill store and a 4-unit small residential building on the property to make way for an 8-story, 172-unit apartment community.
Rendering of the 12th Ave project (Image: PCP)

The Belmont Ave Goodwill project is positioned as a premier, luxury market-rate development targeting high-income urban renters rather than a dedicated income-restricted affordable housing community. PCP emphasizes a high-end, “best-in-class” product intended to capture rental demand from professionals tied to the nearby First Hill medical hub, downtown Seattle, and regional tech employers via light rail.

During pre-development, the site’s commercial and residential tenants will generate approximately $44,000 per month in interim operating revenue, subsidizing land-loan interest ahead of demolition, PCP says.
PCP says the permitting process has been underway and that the Master Use Permit review covering zoning, civil engineering, SEPA, and design review is projected to require roughly 18 months.

The company’s announcement describes urgency to strike while the iron is hot. “PCP’s development strategy is intended to take advantage of the improving Seattle economy at a time where construction starts have dropped over 80% below the historical high mark,” the firm says.

articles.title: Film Review: ‘You Can See Everything’ Gets Too Close
articles.author: Dom Sinacola
paras: You Can See Everything is a reflection of its own making. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it’s a nearly three-hour documentary about Elizabeth Holmes that struggles under the moral weight of being a three-hour documentary about Elizabeth Holmes. You Can See Everything is basically a chamber drama chronicling the making of You Can See Everything .

Documentary is a genre typically rife with self-reference. Take recently released The History of Concrete , wherein writer-director John Wilson assembles the film as it plays out on screen, telling the titular history of concrete by figuring out how one even does that. Fielder actually appears in Wilson’s movie, for a cameo that lasts only half a moment, as he produced Wilson’s TV show on HBO. As The History of Concrete progresses, Wilson shows us the pitch meetings filled with bored executives who ultimately deny the film funding, in turn pushing him to determine how anyone even finances a documentary anymore.

Not well, apparently. As Wilson learns, documentaries are especially fraught enterprises when it comes to capitalism. As is the case with all movies, they require exceptional amounts of money to function, but as is not the case with all movies, they represent a gesture at truth—of depicting reality as it happened—in direct conflict with profit motivations and bottom lines.

Much of what happens in You Can See Everything begins with money. Establishing details are simple enough: Elizabeth Holmes, co-founder of Theranos, was found guilty of defrauding investors in January 2022 , following the collapse of her billion-dollar business. The problem was their product, a small diagnostic box purported to be capable of running hundreds of essential tests based on one drop of blood, very clearly did not work. She also had a 12-year relationship with Sunny Balwani , nearly 20 years her senior and co-founder of Theranos, which further eroded public sentiment around her decision-making and leadership capabilities. Rampant misogyny: check.

Holmes subsequently reported to federal prison in May 2023 to carry out an 11-year sentence, but not before she and her husband, Billy Evans, invited Fielder to film their lives with “radical transparency.” They planned to finally show the world that—despite shows like Hulu’s The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried depicting Holmes as a manipulative money-grubber—she was never in it for the money. She never stopped believing in her invention. Holmes wanted to, and still wants to, help people through the unerring power of science.

You Can See Everything proceeds in kind, at least for its first half. Fielder lurks in the background of domestic scenes, directing a film crew but mostly just observing , occasionally asking questions though otherwise trying, and inevitably failing, to stay apart from Holmes’s and Evans’s every day. At first he stays in a motel, but then moves into the couple’s beachfront rental home at their invitation, sharing full-time, unguarded space with them and their two children.

Meanwhile, Oppenheim and his regular Director of Photography David Bolen—with whom Oppenheim shot his previous film Primetime , which debuted less than a month ago—chronicle the months leading up to their subject’s prison stint in quietly seething passages of extreme close-up. Framing the film in a 4:3 academy ratio, they further box in the film’s big portraits. As Fielder studies Holmes’s face, her globular blue eyes dominating all planes of vision, so does the audience study them both, noting tics and twitches and some throughline of communication, some vein of truth, running between documentarian and documented. Fielder’s burgeoning beard whiskers are the size of house plants in the theater. Normal skin stuff, like blemishes, moles, and pocks, take on the vastness of a landscape. You can see everything—if everything were skin-deep.

A curious situationship unfolds, and Fielder grows bolder the more Holmes and Evans accept him into their home. We see this as the three of them sit closer and closer on the couch together, stare longer and longer into each other’s eyes. While the couple prepares to launch what will amount to Theranos 2.0, despite her sentencing, Fielder struggles to question Holmes in a way that will reveal what she really believes—whether she really did intentionally defraud investors or not—eventually having whole conversations about the definition of lying or the proper recollection of a single word.

Even when he can’t say he truly believes her, he appears to feel something for her beyond what he should, aware that certain lines may be blurring. After all, by filming her for so long, he may even feel like he understands Holmes maybe even more than Evans.
But then Holmes goes to prison, and in its second half, You Can See Everything becomes something you may not see coming.

Or maybe you will, at least if you’re familiar with The Rehearsal or Nathan for You, Fielder’s previous TV shows. The latter Fielder references during one of many meals with Holmes and Evans, in an attempt to make a joke about the irony of once hosting a comedy show about business scams and now documenting Holmes, the public’s scapegoat for business scamming at a macro level. The Rehearsal , especially, serves as a blueprint for how Fielder further burrows down the rabbit hole of Holmes’s whole worldview. You Can See Everything takes on the creeping atmosphere of a procedural.

There is so much to spoil about the film’s second half, heroes to meet and villains to interrogate, but the more to be discovered, the better. There are reenactments. If The Rehearsal is any indication, this is just what Fielder does now, staging conversations and remembered interactions with thrilling candor, down to the most mundane details. At one point, he grimaces to recall the particular coffee maker that Holmes and Evans used. That’s definitely the same toaster, though.

Throughout You Can See Everything , Fielder seems to intuit how intrusive he’s being; he’s ready to walk away but just as willing to get too close. Threatening to catch feelings, he may be too ready to sacrifice the distance he needs to make an impartial, unadulterated document of that pivotal time. Then, at seemingly every turn, Holmes’s reality slightly contorts, with Fielder and Oppenheim acquiring new information, reassessing what their purpose ever even was at the outset of the project.
I also frequently pondered Fielder’s hotel budget. “This is,” as someone will inevitably say, “all very complicated.”

Accompanied by both an endlessly soothing series of close-ups and enough coastal panoramas to drown all sense of reality, Fielder and Oppenheim invite us to watch these people’s lives like we’re gazing alongside them at an oil painting, baroque and leaden with brush strokes. And from such close quarters comes one of the most intimate films of the year.
You Can See Everything opens in wide release on Fri Oct 16 .

articles.title: I, Anonymous: Bumper-to-Bummer Traffic
articles.author: Anonymous
paras: I have noticed a disturbing tendency for cars to leave plenty of space between themselves and the car in front of them when waiting at a red light, as if out of politeness. This is not polite; it is thoughtless. This is absolute disregard for any other cars that might want to get through an intersection without being stuck when the light changes.

Nor can it be called a safety focus, because people don’t need space to protect them from a collision when they’re at a halt. As I recall from driver’s ed, it was recommended to have one car length of space per 10 miles an hour of speed. When your speed is 0 mph, I don’t think you need a full—or even half-car length—for safety. It seems like the gaps actually invite pedestrians to cross between cars. Not to mention that not using space may inspire someone to rear-end you.

articles.title: Scarecrow Video’s 2026 Psychotronic Challenge: Week Three
articles.author: Julianne Bell and Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome to October! It’s the most wonderful time of the year, when I mitigate my seasonal depression by going all in on gothic literature and horror films. The good people at the world’s best video store, Scarecrow Video, have put together their 2026 Psychotronic Challenge , which contains 31 prompts for a movie each day throughout the month. The rules are simple: watch at least one film each day that falls under the psychotronic category “in whatever order suits you,” and “have fun and get weird.” Scarecrow defines “psychotronic” as “denoting or relating to a genre of films that typically have a science fiction, horror, or fantasy theme and were made on a low budget.” But the staff also notes that they don’t necessarily subscribe to the “low budget” definition in order to allow more diversity in the selection. “That being said,” they write, “we do like an underdog more often than not” so “you might as well have a lot of fun pushing yourself to new lows.” My colleague Audrey Vann and I compiled a list of our picks for the second week, which includes horny parasites, creepy clown dolls, and killers in baby masks. Stay tuned for our final post next week, and catch up on week one and week two if you haven’t already. Support your local video store, and happy viewing! –Julianne Bell
15. WORKPLACE WHOOPSIE: “O.S.H.A. inspectors are gonna need a whole case of red tape for this day.” Julianne’s pick: The Faculty (1998)

This 1998 high school sci-fi horror movie has a bonkers cast: Clea DuVall, Josh Hartnett, The Pitt star Shawn Hatosy, Jordana Brewster, Elijah Wood, Salma Hayek, and Jon Stewart, just to name a few. It’s also directed and edited by Robert Rodriguez ( From Dusk Till Dawn , Once Upon a Time in Mexico ) with a screenplay by Scream writer Kevin Williamson. The plot revolves around a group of six teens who begin to suspect their teachers are being replaced by parasitic aliens. It’s a fun take on the high school movie, with quick banter, a soundtrack ranging from Garbage to Oasis, and a grotesque alien queen. Duvall’s loner goth girl character, Stokely, is supposed to be straight—yeah, sure.
More ideas: Annihilation (2018), Sunshine (2007), Pontypool (2008), Alien (1979), Bloodsucking Bastards (2015)
16. STAPH ONLY: “Why doesn’t anyone read the warning signs at the biology lab anymore?”

Lauded as “phallic, gruesome, deranged, forbidden and…funny (or was that just me?)” by Charli XCX on Letterboxd, this early David Cronenberg film follows the residents of a luxury high-rise apartment infected by parasites that turn them into sex maniacs. Think about this the next time you have bed bugs and be grateful.
More ideas: The Island of Dr. Moreau (1996), Panic in the Streets (1950), Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978), Variola Vera (1982), The Andromeda Strain (1971), The Last Man on Earth (1964)

17. VIDEO STORE DAY: “This is the big one. Watch something physically rented or bought from an actual video store. If you live in a place that is unfortunate enough not to have one of these archival treasures then watch a movie with a video store scene in it at least. #vivaphysicalmedia” Audrey’s pick: Frankenhooker (1990)

Frank Henenlotter’s Frankenhooker brings together a few of my favorite things: Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein , models who act (the film stars Penthouse ’s August 1986 Pet of the Month, Patty Mullen), and camp icon Shirley Stoler (of The Honeymoon Killers and Seven Beauties ). The lore of this film runs deep—a ratings body representative reportedly told Henenlotter that the film should be rated “S for shit.” And, when it was released on VHS, it mortified rental customers with a sound chip that exclaimed, “Wanna date?” when it was picked up. Needless to say, it’s taken a few decades for this gem of a movie to be appreciated. RENT IT. More ideas: MaXXXine (2024), The Last Video Store (2003), Benny’s Video (1992), Stan Helsing (2009), Scream (1996)
18. CREEPETITION: “Rewatch the first movie you ever saw that really made your skin crawl. Don’t be scared, we got you.”
Julianne’s picks: The Sixth Sense (1999) or The Tooth Fairy (2006)

When I was far too young, I saw a clip on TV of the scene from The Sixth Sense when the ghost of the dead bicyclist with a broken neck from a car accident is standing outside Toni Collette’s car, and it haunted me for years, so I’d probably choose that for this prompt. I was terrified whenever I saw an ambulance after that. The other contender would be 2006’s direct-to-DVD The Tooth Fairy , which I watched at a Halloween party when I was 15. It was very bad, and I mocked it mercilessly, but I was still scared to turn the lights off alone in my room afterward.

Attention parents: Just because Poltergeist is rated PG does not mean it won’t haunt your children for the rest of their lives. I first saw the film—upon the recommendation of my dad—when I was seven years old, and when that ghost-hunting assistant peeled his face off in the bathroom mirror, the image was burned into my memory and kept in a special compartment of my brain along with Large Marge ( Pee Wee’s Big Adventure ) and Martian Girl ( Mars Attacks! ). Is there swearing in Poltergeist? No. Is there excessive gore? Also no. But there is a creepy clown doll that giggles and moves sometimes, and for that reason, it should be rated R.

19. DISCHARGE: “Hey hey, ho ho, that nasty ooze has got to go! *You see, the only truly great jokes are the ones that have to be over-explained right? Check it out… In addition to being a less than flattering name for bodily fluid secretions, Discharge is also the name of a 1970’s/80’s minimalistic UK punk band with intense drone-like rhythms who sing short sharp protest songs, mostly about the fears and horrors of nuclear war and the fallout from it. Some have described their sound as a “grave-black aural acid assault.” How is that for information leakage? Haha. We suppose you could opt for a film about nuclear fallout, war, punk stuff, or just plain ol’ seepage of some sort.” Julianne’s pick: Green Room (2015)

In A24’s critically acclaimed horror-thriller Green Room , the fictional punk band the Ain’t Rights, composed of bassist Pat (the late Anton Yelchin), guitarist Sam (Alia Shawkat), drummer Reece (Joe Cole), and singer Tiger (Callum Turner), are touring the Pacific Northwest when a series of misadventures leads them to grudgingly perform at a neo-Nazi bar outside Portland. After the members witness a stabbing committed by a member of the Nazi metal headliner in the venue’s green room, they find themselves locked in a grim battle for their lives, fighting a gang of “red lace” skinheads tooth and nail alongside the murder victim’s friend Amber (Imogen Poots). Everyone in the main ensemble delivers powerful performances, but Patrick Stewart is particularly chilling as the aloof white supremacist bar owner, Darcy.
More ideas: Slime City (1988), The Blob (1988), The Stuff (1985), The Blob (1958), The Fly (1986), The Substance (2024)
20. MAN, YOU GOT SOME ‘SPLAINING TO WATCH: “Characters, or even whole movies, who feel compelled to explain everything. ‘Educate’ yourself with one of those.”

For a long time, I misjudged the Scream franchise as a cheesy batch of jump-scare cash grabs. Now, I see the truth: the films strike a perfect balance of astute horror satire and camp high school drama. The first Scream film remains my favorite, as it has the incredible outfits (Rose McGowan’s psychedelic miniskirt is everything to me), queer subtext (Billy and Stu 4ever
More ideas: It Follows (2014), The Cabin in the Woods (2011), Nosferatu (2024), Happy Death Day 2U (2019), Heretic (2024)
21. BACK TO THE FUTURE DAY: “Really though, any time travel flick will do the trick.”

What’s better than a time loop movie? A horror time loop movie! Happy Death Day is the ideal mix of comedy and slasher and a great comfort watch (if you’re a sicko like me who finds horror movies soothing). After superficial sorority girl Tree Gelbman (played flawlessly by Jessica Rothe) is stabbed on her birthday by a killer in a creepy baby mask, she is forced to live the last day of her life over and over until she can solve the mystery of her own murder.
More ideas: Triangle (2009), The Final Girls (2015), The Girl Who Leapt Through Time (2006), Time Masters (1982), Lost Highway (1997)
