articles.title: 2026 General Election Endorsements
articles.author: Elections Committee
paras: This midterm election will be a big deal, and not just because Democrats could retake Congress from Republicans and provide a check on Trump’s power at the federal level. A ton of interesting races and measures are also brewing at the local level. Ballots should be arriving in mailboxes by October 16 across Washington state.

It’s imperative that we block megamillionaire Brian Heywood’s latest Eymanesque effort to hijack Washington state’s legislative process through ballot initiative campaigns he and his rich friends bankroll. Their top goal this session seems to be to repeal the millionaires tax, and the benefit to them is obvious. The question is what does lowering taxes on multimillionaires get the rest of us?

As a side quest to their tax the rich repeal battle, Heywood’s campaign also seeks to force schools to turn over kids’ medical records, even if they’re parents are charged with abuse. Plus, they want to inspect your kids’ genitals before they can play sports. This is in the name of the alleged scourge of trans women competing in school sports, but it’s a solution in search of a problem, with a massive amount of harmful side effects. Vote no on all three statewide initiatives from these creepy multimillionaires.

Meanwhile, Washington State’s congressional delegation did not exactly inspire us with confidence that they will be leading the charge to defang Trump, and too few long-time incumbents drew credible challenges. Further down the ticket, however, we see plenty of exciting candidates – some even daring to challenge powerful incumbents and force them to defend how they are adapting to our present political moment.

The progress being made in Olympia stands in stark contrast to intractable federal gridlock on key issues and increasing democratic backsliding. In a productive period from 2023 to 2025, state lawmakers phased out single family zoning in favor of more affordable middle housing, enacted rent stabilization, reformed parking mandates, and barred cities from broadly banning apartments near our biggest transit investments.
Find our endorsements useful? Donate to support our Election Committee's work and our local reporting that informs it.

The Washington State Legislature is fresh off passing a millionaires tax that will help ease the burden on the working class once it goes into effect in 2029. We were impressed by the broad coalition that advanced the tax, which only hits those who earn more than $1 million in compensation per year, and convinced Governor Bob Ferguson (hardly known for his boldness or backbone) to get behind the effort.

Unfortunately, after queuing up the millionaires’ tax, Ferguson has settled back into his lane of opposing new efforts to tax the rich and focusing the agenda on cuts to state programs. We do not think the work of progressive tax reform is done, and we want to see the state do more to invest in our future, whether expanding public transit, investing in affordable housing, ensuring universal health care, or meeting the state’s paramount duty to ensure the “ample provision for the education of all children.”

Our slate of candidates for the state House and Senate is ready to continue that work, and we’re excited to see what our state can accomplish when it sheds outmoded constraints, like a car-centric approach to infrastructure investments or an instilled fear of taxing the rich.

Oh and did we mention control of the Seattle City Council could also be up for grabs due to a special election in District 5? With centrists still holding a grip on council, progressive legislation continues to face a fraught path forward. Whether Mayor Katie Wilson gets a chance to deliver on campaign promises to make Seattle a more affordable and safe place to live could depend on electing progressive councilmembers, like Nilu Jenks, who [spoiler alert] we enthusiastically endorsed in the D5 race. Read on to see why.

Ballots should be arriving in your mail boxes this week. Washington voters have until 8pm Tuesday, November 3 to return a ballot at a drop box or get it postmarked. Visit the Vote WA portal to register or check your voter information.

The 2026 Elections Committee is led by chairs Forrest Baum and Kelsey Vanhee. Membership includes Tamer Abouzeid, Mike Bollich-Ziegler, Angela Compton, Austin Field, Caitlin Hepworth, Amber Hu, Naomi Lewis, Oliver Moffat, Ryan Packer, Maya Ramakrishnan, Jazmine Smith, and Doug Trumm.
Find our endorsements useful? Donate to support our Election Committee's work and our local reporting that informs it.
Urbanists will join the long list of groups voting “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 (aka the “Parents’ Bill of Rights”).

Sadly, not all kids live in homes that are safe and accepting, and for some vulnerable kids, teachers and school counselors may be the only safe grownups in their lives. Right-wingers have long worked to dismantle public education and attack the educators and staff who work to protect victims of child abuse and LGBTQ+ kids.

Hedge fund manager Brian Heywood is back again trying to trick voters into passing his so-called “Parents’ Bill of Rights” — officially titled “Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.” This badly written initiative would force schools to involuntarily “out” LGBTQ+ kids and strip privacy from child abuse victims.

Voters might be wondering why this scrap of rage bait has risen again. A few years ago, Heywood’s Let’s Go Washington PAC hired signature gatherers to get the first “Parent’s Rights” initiative certified. That original version tried to trick voters into stripping student privacy protections by hiding it within a long list of already existing “Parental Rights”.

But the state legislature defused Heywood’s sneak attack by simply adopting all the duplicative rules while still protecting the privacy of vulnerable children. Now Heywood and his MAGA buddies have once more crawled from under a rock and hired signature gatherers to place their “Parental Rights” initiative back on the ballot.

Urbanists won’t be fooled: this initiative has nothing to do with protecting kids and families. If approved by voters, I-001 would force schools to turn over private records about child abuse victims to their parental abusers. Even parents under criminal investigation for sexual abuse of their child would gain access to private school counseling records.

By requiring schools to disclose highly confidential mental health counseling files to parents, I-001 forces school counselors to “out” vulnerable LGBTQ+ kids to their families. Because of family rejection, LGBTQ+ children (especially trans kids) are more likely to experience homelessness than other kids and are at higher risk of self-harm than other kids.
This cruel Initiative would strip kids’ privacy, causing family conflict, increased youth homelessness, and worsen the teen mental illness crisis. Vote “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.

Mandatory sex inspections of young girls is not a phrase any of us wants to be writing, any of you want to be reading, or anyone should ever want to require. This initiative, bafflingly, claims to be about “defending equity in interscholastic sports” while prohibiting a tiny number of trans students from participating in sports and subjecting all girls to a mandatory inspection to confirm their biological sex.

Still need a reason to vote no? No Hate in Washington State calls I-638 “The most extreme MAGA measure of its kind in the U.S., I-638 would require tens of thousands of elementary, middle and high school girls (but not boys) to undergo intrusive, potentially harmful medical sex inspections every year as a new part of sports physicals.”

Call us old-fashioned, but we think youth sports are supposed to be about having fun, encouraging physical activity, teamwork, and leadership skills, not about unnecessary and invasive medical inspections or imposed gender conformity. We’re proud to join the Washington State PTA , the Washington Education Association , League of Women Voters , and many, many more in opposing this awful initiative. Vote no on I-638.
Find our endorsements useful? Donate to support our Election Committee's work and our local reporting that informs it.

We’ve been screaming from the rooftops for years that if we want to get this state on track, we absolutely must fix our regressive, upside-down tax code. It’s also wildly popular and works like a charm . It’s why we support the capital gains tax and defended it when hedge fund manager Brian Heywood tried to repeal it in 2024. And it’s why the millionaires tax is another huge step forward in making meaningful change in our struggling state budget so that we can continue to have the way of life in Washington that people love.

Like the attempted capital gains tax repeal, this new attack on the millionaires tax would upend our budget if passed and defund our schools and healthcare. The ballot measure, listed as IP26-645, was forced onto the ballot by a multi-million-dollar signature-gathering campaign funded by Haywood and his rich friends, hoping to shrink their tax bills – even though the richest 1% already pay a lower tax rate than the vast majority of middle-class Washingtonians.

First, let’s get some facts straight. This tax is narrower than simply being a millionaire: the tax applies to income over a million dollars per year (less than 20,000 households) and would only apply after that millionth dollar. If you make $1,000,100 in one year, your tax burden would be $9.90.

Despite that narrow pool and large deduction, it’s projected to bring in over $3 billion per year to fund schools, child care, healthcare, and reduce/eliminate other taxes everyday people pay. In other words: with the millionaires tax, most people pay less in taxes, small businesses pay less in taxes, and the ultrawealthy pay a little bit more towards their fair share. Without it, we lose big on the things that matter most to us.

What would you do with a million extra bus hours? Well, the Seattle Transit Measure is investing them in more frequency, more weekend service, more midday service, and more late-night service. Plus, the transit measure would fund more free ORCA passes for low-income riders. This renewal would take all of the bonus investments that Seattle has infused into Metro service and amplify it, in addition to funding the streetcar system and more.

Everyone should be able to get to where they’re going at any time of day in a world-class city like Seattle. We deserve to be able to make it to the kids’ soccer games on weekends, make it home from a night out or a late shift, and have regular, frequent service throughout the day.

Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposal doubles the size of the transit measure, raising about $138 million annually by increasing the measure’s sales tax from 0.15% to 0.3%. That would give Seattle extra purchasing power, with 280,000 bus service hours to invest annually instead of the 180,000 previously. Seattle and Metro expect at least 10 of the city’s busiest buses to see augmented service over current levels.

Because this is a renewal of existing revenue, if the measure were to fail, we would lose funds, lose service hours, lose frequency, and lose big altogether. While sales taxes are regressive, cutting bus service is far more regressive.
Hop on board, Seattle. Vote Yes on Prop 1.

Just as critically, Pierce County absolutely must pass its own transit measure . It’s also a small sales tax increase, but it would similarly mean more buses, running to more places, more often. It also makes buses fare-free for seniors. So much good would come of the investments into Pierce Transit that this measure enables.
Prop 1 would increase service levels by more than 40%, a massive infusion for a county that has lagged behind on transit investment.

If approved, the ballot measure would bump the dedicated sales tax rate funding Pierce Transit from 0.6% to 0.9%, a funding stream that has been sitting unchanged since George W. Bush's first term in the White House. That would put Pierce County in closer parity with neighboring counties, which boast more frequent bus service.

With the added funding, Pierce Transit expects to be able to add four brand new routes across Tacoma and Puyallup, extend hours on 23 routes, and boost frequencies on 21 routes to run at least every 20 to 30 minutes on the weekends, compared to just four routes clearing that basic bar for frequency today.

When we think about how people get around, where they get around and how we can connect communities across the sound, Pierce has to be a part of that picture. It’s not just about Tacoma. Whether you live in Puyallup or Gig Harbor, Steilacoom or Fife, you deserve transit access and reliable service.

While Seattle often passes transit funding measures by comfortable margins, the same is not true of Pierce County, which saw its last transit measures fail in 2011 and 2012. It’s going to be a tight race to get it passed, so it’s important to vote yes and talk to your neighbors about how important it is that they do, too!

articles.title: 'The Ave for All' Transforms U District's Main Thoroughfare
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seeing a street festival take over University Way NE through the heart of the U District is a common sight throughout most of the year. But this past Saturday, the attraction wasn't food vendors or craftspeople – it was the street itself. Visitors to one of the city's most beloved shopping districts were treated to a fully pedestrianized street as part of " The Ave for All ", which continues this upcoming Saturday, October 17 for a second weekend.

An idea advanced by the placemaking group U District Advocates, The Ave for All gives pedestrians breathing room to enjoy a leisurely Saturday without being crammed onto University Way's narrow sidewalks. Tables and chairs turned the periphery of the street into a patio that wasn't tied to any specific businesses, prompting more folks to stick around and linger... but also grab a bite nearby.

Games, including a large chess board, provided activation and a pair of buskers livened the mood. It didn't hurt that storm clouds, spitting rain in the early afternoon, cleared away and left a beautiful autumn day.
For event organizer L. Harrison Jerome, the Ave for All is a glimpse of how a neighborhood like the University District can better use one of its biggest stretches of real estate – the street.

"In this neighborhood, you see how thin the sidewalks are. Now people actually have the ability to move out into the space, and they're actually filling it," Jerome told The Urbanist. "They're doing chalk art, they're hanging out with each other, they're playing games, they're having off street dining. It's really, really nice weather today, and people are just enjoying the street in a different way than they had before."

As a broader city, Seattle is taking small steps toward creating more pedestrian-oriented spaces out of underutilized stretches of roadway, with the Seattle Department of Transportation's People Streets and Public Spaces program at the forefront of that work. Potential public plazas are being eyed in the Admiral District, Delridge, and on Upper Queen Anne, projects that will ultimately be demonstrations of the idea of creating a pedestrian plaza at the heart of every neighborhood.
But The Ave for All is presenting a bolder vision of how a street at the heart of a business district can truly transform.

U District Advocates has pointed out that they are not the first group to dream of a fully pedestrian-oriented Ave, with storied Seattle architect Victor Steinbrueck putting the idea forward in 1955. The idea got closest to becoming a reality in the early 1970s, with the University District Development Council established specifically to advance the idea.

"The plan basically calls for a pedestrian mall on University Way NE to run from NE 47th to NE 42nd streets," a February 1972 story in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer noted. At that time, outgoing UDDC Executive Vice President David Rowlands touted the proposal for a U District pedestrian mall as creating "what Ghirardelli Square is to San Francisco, what the French Quarter is to New Orleans and what George-town is to Washington, D.C."

The year before in 1971, UDDC surveyed participants at the U District Street Fair finding 90% general support for the idea of a pedestrian mall ( sound familiar? ). But the proposal fell apart when property owners on the Ave were required to provide their stamp of approval. An alternative proposal put forward by neighborhood real estate broker Don Kennedy included a pedestrian plaza in front of what is now the UW tower connected to a "tremendous" parking garage with shops on top. That idea never came to fruition either.

Everything old is new again. Earlier this summer, the U District Advocates had a false start after the City of Seattle declined to approve an initial request to open up the Ave in late May and early June , with a number of nearby business owners opposing the plan.

As the Seattle Times reported at the time, the push back was orchestrated by Lois Ko and Emily Scully, owners of Sweet Alchemy and Shultzy’s Bar & Grill respectively. But after other business owners in the neighborhood found they'd been added to a list of opponents of the event without their knowledge, a cloud of animus and uncertainty grew up around the entire project that threatened to sour the spirit of The Ave for All.

While that's not exactly ancient history at this point, it did seem to be put in the rearview mirror this weekend. For the autumn re-do, U District Advocates was asked to jump through a few more hoops to show they'd conducted community outreach, a bar they were ultimately able to clear.

"One thing I learned from that it's sort of difficult for community groups to do things like this," Jerome said. "We know that there's a huge amount of support for reprioritizing a ton of our streets back toward people rather than cars, but it's really difficult for people to voice those wants."

What the future holds for The Ave is impossible to know. But based on the turnout this past weekend, there's clear demand for something to draw people out into the street, even without a food festival.

"We'd love to do this event again," Jerome said. "We want to work with the City and the businesses and the local community, the residents, the students, get everybody in the conversation to actually talk about what a city pilot of this could actually look like, where we do it day-to-day or on weekends, sometime in the spring or the summer."
U District residents and visitors will have one more chance to visit The Ave for All this Saturday from 11am to 8pm.

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
